pages.brief: In a tropical rainforest in Asia, the real giant ape Gigantopithecus stands on its hind legs and eats bamboo, fruit, and seeds. Some males are 10 feet tall and weigh more than 1,000 pounds; females are half that size. An early human, Homo erectus, may live nearby.

pages.text: An African elephant (left) stands with the woolly mammoth and three of their closely related ancestors. How are they different from each other? Mammuthus — Woolly Mammoth and Its Relatives Time to move forward again to between 4 million and 10,000 years ago, during the last ice age, to catch a glimpse of a woolly mammoth, a species of Mammuthus. Keep your eyes peeled for a creature that looks like a huge, hairy elephant with long, curved tusks. There it is, using its tusks to clear paths through snow, probably searching for plants. The woolly mammoth stands almost 12 feet (3.6 m) tall, but another Mammuthus species can grow as tall as 14 feet (4.3 m). Early humans hunt mammoths and paint pictures of them, which can still be seen on cave walls in modern Europe. Mammoths will become extinct at the end of the ice age, when the weather becomes too warm for them.
pages.brief: During the last ice age, a woolly mammoth uses its long, curved tusks to clear paths through snow while searching for plants. The huge hairy elephant stands almost 12 feet tall, and another Mammuthus species grows even taller. An African elephant and three close relatives stand nearby for comparison.

pages.text: Megatherium — Giant Ground Sloth Don’t take off your winter coat yet. Another huge mammal that lives during the last ice age is Megatherium, a giant ground sloth. It lives about 2 million to 8,000 years ago and is almost 20 feet (6 m) long. Megatherium is related to the much smaller tree sloths that live in South America today. The one you’re watching is standing on its hind legs, using its tail for balance, which shouldn’t surprise you. Fossil footprints found in your time show that it could stand and even walk upright. Megatherium had hard, bony plates (like the armadillo’s) under its long fur. The plates helped protect it from attacks by other animals.
pages.brief: During the last ice age, the giant ground sloth Megatherium stands on its hind legs and uses its tail for balance. It is almost 20 feet long and related to much smaller tree sloths. Hard bony plates under its long fur protect it from attacks.

pages.text: A World Without Giants? Isn’t it amazing to think that giants such as the ones in this book once walked on Earth and swam in the ocean? It’s too bad we can’t see these huge creatures today. However, you don’t have to get in a time machine to see gigantic animals. Blue whales, great white sharks, giant squids, grizzly bears, elephants, giraffes, ostriches, condors, and anacondas are some of the large animals that share the planet with us today. Unfortunately, many of these animals are threatened with extinction. It’s important to protect these animals, mainly by preserving their habitats. That way, we can be sure that we’ll never live in a world without giants. How We Compare Today feet human rhinoceros African elephant giraffe.
pages.brief: Blue whales, great white sharks, giant squids, grizzly bears, elephants, giraffes, ostriches, condors, and anacondas share the planet with people today. Many of these large animals are threatened with extinction, so preserving their habitats is important. A size comparison shows humans beside a rhinoceros, African elephant, and giraffe.

pages.text: (adj.) page 4 of or relating to the time before recorded or written history species (n.) page 4 a group of living things that are physically similar and can reproduce tentacles (n.) page 7 long, flexible limbs on an animal, especially an invertebrate trilobites (n.) page 7 common prehistoric sea animals that were covered with a soft shell.
pages.brief: A glossary page presents four key terms from the book with short definitions: prehistoric, species, tentacles, and trilobites. The entries explain life before written history, similar living things that can reproduce, flexible animal limbs, and common prehistoric sea animals with soft shells.

books.title: The Case of the Disappearing Honeybees
books.art_why: The book is about real honeybees, hives, farms, scientists and modern events, so photographs fit.

pages.text: The Case of the Disappearing Honeybees.
pages.brief: A honeybee colony surrounds a wooden hive in a flower-filled meadow, introducing the mystery of disappearing honeybees. Warm sunlight and green foliage frame the bees as they move around their home. The scene is calm and natural.

pages.text: A healthy honeybee colony moves into a new hive. Who Took My Strawberries? Think of your favorite fruit. Now imagine a world in which that fruit—and many other fruits, nuts, vegetables, and flowers— is extremely rare, perhaps even nonexistent. Such would be the world without honeybees. Honeybees don’t just make honey. They pollinate the blossoms of plants. One in three bites of the food people enjoy is the product of honeybees’ hard labor. Yet, in 2007, honeybee populations began to decline rapidly. The reason has puzzled scientists for years. Although the problem slowed over time, the mystery of what caused it in the first place remains. Researchers are still working today to help save the honeybees.
pages.brief: A healthy honeybee colony moves into a new hive while strawberries and other fruits, nuts, vegetables and flowers appear in a world that would be scarce without honeybees. Bees pollinate blossoms, showing one in three bites of food depends on their work.

pages.text: Busy Bees Honeybees live in colonies, busy places where each bee performs a specialized task. All the bees in a colony depend on one another and must work together to keep the hive humming. Outside the colony, a lone honeybee isn’t likely to survive for more than twenty-four hours. Honeybee activity outside the hive is dedicated to a single purpose—finding flowers in bloom and collecting pollen from them for food as well as nectar to make honey. Honeybees from a single, healthy hive can visit more than 100,000 flowers in a day while performing one of the most critical processes in nature: pollination. When a bee brushes against the anthers on the inside of a flower, the bee’s body picks up pollen grains from that flower. The pollen is transferred to the pistils of other flowers as the bee makes its rounds from blossom to blossom. The ongoing transfer of pollen from anthers to pistils is pollination, leading to fertilization, a process that will eventually result in seed formation. anthers pollen pistil.
pages.brief: Inside a busy colony, honeybees perform specialized tasks and depend on one another. Outside, a lone bee visits blossoms, brushing against anthers and picking up pollen grains. The bee carries pollen from anther to pistil on other flowers, completing pollination that leads to fertilization and seed formation.

pages.text: Without pollination, plants don’t reproduce. They eventually die off without being replaced, which presents a serious problem for animals that rely on those plants as a food source. Missing in Action The problem of disappearing honeybees became evident in October 2006, when an American commercial beekeeper arrived at one of his apiaries in Florida to retrieve four hundred hives. Three weeks before, the hives had appeared active and healthy, but now they were empty except for food, baby bees, and a few queens. The beekeeper surveyed his surroundings, expecting to see piles of dead insects littering the ground, but there was no sign of the twenty million bees that had disappeared. A frame from a honeybee colony before and after the bees vanished. This beekeeper’s experience, it turns out, was not unique. Reports of other losses began to surface across the United States, Europe, China, and other regions. The numbers were shocking.
pages.brief: A commercial beekeeper arrives at a Florida apiary to retrieve four hundred hives. The hives are empty except for food, baby bees and a few queens. He surveys the ground for dead insects but finds no sign of twenty million missing bees. A frame shows a colony before and after the bees vanished.

pages.text: During the winter of 2006–2007, roughly 750,000 of the estimated 2.4 million bee colonies in the United States had vanished. On average, U.S. beekeepers lost 38 percent of their colonies. The largest known disappearance occurred during 2008 in the almond tree groves of California, where two billion bees vanished. Faced with an emerging crisis, farmers and beekeepers were desperate for science to shed some light on the mystery. On the Case Scientists named the problem colony collapse disorder (CCD) and began documenting its symptoms. CCD happens in a matter of weeks when most of the occupants of what seems to be a healthy hive suddenly vanish. Few, if any, dead bees from the colony can be found. The only bees remaining are the very young and the queen— members of the colony that normally would never be left alone by the rest of the bees. Once the symptoms of CCD were identified, the real detective work began. Scientists from around the country set out to determine the cause of the disorder and propose a solution. CCD scientists surveyed beekeepers and collected samples of wax, pollen, and live and dead bees (when they could be found). When scientists.
pages.brief: During winter, hundreds of thousands of U.S. bee colonies have vanished, and beekeepers lose many hives. In California almond groves, two billion bees disappear. Scientists name the problem colony collapse disorder and document hives where only the queen and very young bees remain, with few dead bees found.

pages.text: Next, scientists considered germs known to damage bees’ immune systems. Scientists found fungal bacteria that made it difficult for bees to eat and left them too weak to forage. They also detected a variation of a well-known fatal pathogen called acute bee paralysis virus (ABPV) in a large number of CCD hives. Yet efforts to pinpoint a single germ as the root cause of the bees’ demise led nowhere. Everything they had looked at seemed to be the result of CCD rather than its cause. The scientists next turned their attention to several parasites. One, an ominously named mite called Varroa destructor, is also known as the “vampire mite.” It clings to adult bees, sucking their blood and leaving them with open wounds that make them susceptible to infection. A scientist takes samples from a hive with CCD.
pages.brief: Scientists dissect honeybees and find multiple diseases, suggesting compromised immune systems. They examine germs, fungal bacteria and a fatal paralysis virus in CCD hives. A scientist takes samples from a hive. Researchers also study parasites, including the Varroa destructor mite that clings to adult bees and sucks their blood.

pages.text: Average Annual Hive Loss by State, 2020–2021 Another parasite, called Nosema apis, has an equally gruesome effect on honeybee health. This parasite produces spores that infect the bees’ intestines and essentially eat the bee from the inside out. These parasites, however, had been observed in hives before. Whatever was triggering CCD seemed to be coming from another source. Just One Crop Researchers decided to look beyond the bees and their hives. They began looking at how farming practices had changed. Years ago, most farms were small, family-run operations that grew and harvested a variety of crops.
pages.brief: A parasite called Nosema apis produces spores that infect honeybee intestines and damage the bee from inside. Scientists compare this with earlier hive losses and look beyond the bees and hives. They begin examining how farming practices have changed, seeking another source for colony collapse disorder.

pages.text: Today, many farms are massive corporate operations engaged in monoculture—farming that specializes in a single crop, such as wheat, corn, or soybeans. Monoculture farming is simple and efficient for farmers, but it certainly isn’t good for bees. Cultivating a single crop results in a single blooming season, which leaves bees in that area with no source of pollen or nectar once those flowers fade. Bees must also contend with exposure to chemical pesticides intended to rid fields of other insects that might destroy an entire harvest. While pesticides used correctly can save crops, they can also spell trouble for bees, which use their bodies to filter out toxins from the honey they produce. It’s challenging for farmers to find chemical pesticides that kill harmful insects but leave the beneficial ones alone. In the United States, farmers try to spray crops at times when plants aren’t blooming in an effort to keep bees safe. Yet even with these precautions, scientists still found pesticides in the samples they’d collected from hives with CCD. According to the Environmental Protection Agency, more than a billion pounds of chemicals are used on our crops annually. Scientists have.
pages.brief: Large corporate farms practice monoculture, growing a single crop such as wheat, corn or soybeans. One blooming season leaves bees without pollen or nectar once flowers fade. Bees also face chemical pesticides sprayed on fields. Scientists find pesticides in samples from CCD hives even when farmers spray when plants are not blooming.

pages.text: A new class of pesticides called neonicotinoids or neonics has some scientists particularly concerned. These pesticides are systemic. Plant seeds are treated with chemicals that then spread to every part of a plant as it grows. A single neonics treatment is long-lasting and kills various crop pests, as it should, but researchers discovered what appeared to be an unintended consequence of using these treatments—a rapid rise in CCD. Life Without the Birds and the Bees—The Great Sparrow Campaign In 1958, Mao Zedong, the founding father of the People’s Republic of China, kicked off the Great Sparrow Campaign. Hundreds of millions of sparrows were killed throughout China because the sparrows ate grain that Zedong thought could feed Chinese people instead. However, the birds also ate insects. Without the sparrows, locusts consumed human crops. As many as 45 million people starved. This led China to use more pesticides. Parts of China now use so many chemicals that bees have all disappeared. Farm workers must do the bees’ job for them. They use cotton swabs to hand-pollinate fruit trees, bloom by bloom.
pages.brief: A new class of systemic pesticides called neonicotinoids is used on seeds and spreads through every part of a growing plant. Researchers see a rapid rise in CCD. In China, after sparrows were killed, locusts consumed crops; heavy pesticide use followed, and farm workers now hand-pollinate fruit trees with cotton swabs.

pages.text: Scientists wonder if systemic pesticides might weaken the bees’ immune systems, allowing pathogens like the paralysis virus to take hold. It’s also possible that, since the pesticides affect the nervous system, they might interfere with the bees’ ability to learn, remember, and navigate. This could explain the bees’ failure to return to the hive after foraging. It seems logical to draw these conclusions since the introduction of these new pesticides coincides with the appearance of CCD, but the overlap in timing is not enough to suggest that the pesticides actually cause CCD. In fact, recent research says otherwise. Researchers are now becoming even more convinced that the onset of CCD does not have a single cause but may instead result from a combination of factors. Keep On Trucking Scientists continued to explore other factors that could contribute to CCD, including a form of job stress. Bees have been buzzing around the world for 150 million years, but in the last 10,000 years the relationship between bees and humans has transformed. Humans went from being foragers of naturally pollinated food to using bees for monoculture farming. People can control where and when honeybees work.
pages.brief: Scientists wonder whether systemic pesticides weaken bee immune systems, letting pathogens like paralysis virus take hold. Pesticides may affect bee nervous systems and interfere with learning, memory and navigation, so bees fail to return after foraging. Researchers now suspect CCD has no single cause but results from a combination of factors.

pages.text: Do You Know? Ancient Egyptians floated beehives on rafts down the Nile River to follow the bloom. Today, trucks like this one transport hives all over the country. Since honeybees are excellent pollinators, moving them into a field while crops are blooming is a way for farmers to ensure a plentiful harvest. Today in the United States, semi-trailer trucks transport hives from one farm to another all over the country. The honeybees they haul pollinate $15 billion worth of food annually in the United States alone. The thought of trucking a million bees down the highway may seem strange, but it helps production with modern monoculture farming. Farmers might need bees to pollinate one crop in February and another one in a different part of the country in April. Almond trees, for example, are completely dependent on honeybees for pollination.
pages.brief: Ancient Egyptians float beehives on rafts down the Nile to follow the bloom. Today, semi-trailer trucks transport hives across the United States so honeybees pollinate crops, including fifteen billion dollars’ worth of food each year. The trucks help modern monoculture farming, where farmers need bees for different crops in different places.

pages.text: Around Valentine’s Day, bees are trucked to the California groves, and they go to work when the almond trees start to bloom. For two weeks, those 600,000 acres (242,811 ha) of blooming trees are a bustling and beautiful sight. The call for pollination services continued to increase, and managed honeybee colonies declined rapidly to very low numbers. Once the blossoms are gone, the bees are packed up and shipped to a new location. Transport is tough on the bees since they are shut inside trucks with no way to obtain flower nectar. The sugar water that beekeepers feed them instead is comparable to junk food. Millions of bees die from the stress of commuting from job to job. Which Crops Need Bees Most?
pages.brief: Around Valentine’s Day, trucks carry bees to California almond groves. For two weeks, six hundred thousand acres of blooming almond trees are a bustling, beautiful sight. Then the bees are packed up and shipped to a new location. Shut inside trucks with only sugar water, millions die from the stress of commuting from job to job.

pages.text: Migrant bees face another problem— contagion. When bees arrive at their next pollination job, they come in contact with millions of other migrant-worker bees. By one estimate, two-thirds of all bees in the United States interact on these huge farms. Bringing in bees from different parts of the country (or world) also spreads parasites and disease at a rapid rate, as they travel cross-country along with the honeybees. In the United States, beekeepers have attempted to fend off disease by adding antibiotics to the sugar water that the bees feed on as they travel. Using antibiotics as a preventive measure, however, creates a problem of its own. Overuse of antibiotics may have weakened the honeybees’ ability to fight other diseases and resist the effects of pesticides. The drugs also kill off beneficial bacteria that help the honeybees process food. An additional concern is that, over time, bacteria can build up resistance to antibiotics, which renders the drugs ineffective. The hazards of migratory beekeeping are just one more piece of the complex puzzle of CCD. As with any puzzle, every piece matters. It looked more and more as though CCD was a complicated mix of biological, chemical, and physical stresses.
pages.brief: Migrant bees meet millions of other migrant-worker bees on huge farms, spreading parasites and disease quickly across the country. Beekeepers add antibiotics to sugar water during travel, but overuse may weaken bees, kill beneficial bacteria and help bacteria become resistant. The hazards of migratory beekeeping are one more piece of the complex CCD puzzle.

pages.text: Help the Bees Because of the complexity of CCD, scientists have yet to pinpoint an exact cause or a complete cure. However, they have improved prevention measures and discovered some promising treatments. As a result, the rates of CCD have dropped over time—though not as much as scientists would like. Solving the case of the disappearing honeybees once and for all will require additional research. In the meantime, we can use the available knowledge and resources to foster bee-friendly environments that will benefit plants, bees, and people. Africanized Survivors In some places, bee species seem to be breeding and evolving into stronger strains. For instance, the Africanized honeybee is a hybrid of the European honeybee and the African honeybee. Some of these bees escaped from a Brazilian lab in 1957 and spread north, reaching the United States in 1990. People were horrified. Africanized bees are more aggressive than European honeybees, and rumors spread that they didn’t make honey or pollinate plants. In fact, they do both those things. The bees are more defensive, but they are also healthier. Some beekeepers began to welcome them as nature’s answer to CCD.
pages.brief: Scientists have not found an exact cause or complete cure for CCD, but prevention and promising treatments have helped rates drop. Africanized honeybees, a hybrid that escaped from a Brazilian lab in 1957 and reached the United States in 1990, are more aggressive but healthier; some beekeepers welcome them as nature’s answer to CCD.

pages.text: Honeybees benefit from access to a diversity of plant life; having a variety of native wildflowers gives honeybees a longer foraging season. People can create honeybee sanctuaries in their yards— places full of blooming native plants where bees can reduce their contact with pesticides and thrive in a natural environment. Rooftop and backyard pollinator gardens are gaining popularity in many rural and urban neighborhoods. The bees visit parks and gardens, producing honey and pollinating native fruit trees and plants. What Lawns Lack While colony collapse disease is in decline, another bee crisis is on the rise. Many species of native bees are endangered and at risk of extinction. Manicured lawns have contributed to wild bee decline. Certain types of bees rely on certain plants to survive. Because there are fewer native plants and more honeybees—which farmers bring in to pollinate crops—wild bees are having trouble finding food and shelter.
pages.brief: Honeybees benefit from a diversity of plant life and native wildflowers that give a longer foraging season. People create honeybee sanctuaries in yards and rooftop or backyard pollinator gardens. The bees visit parks and gardens, produce honey and pollinate native fruit trees. Native wild bees, however, are endangered as manicured lawns reduce wild plants.

pages.text: Even commercial monoculture farmers can find small ways to help bees without sacrificing a productive harvest. Setting aside a small portion of their land for native plants that would sustain bees all year long instead of just for a couple of weeks each year would help create a population of homegrown pollinators. Farmers could even investigate more organic means of pest control that would let them avoid using toxic chemicals to deal with pests. Bees are small but important contributors to the health and well-being of many other species, including humans. Taking action to protect them helps not only the bees but us as well.
pages.brief: Commercial monoculture farmers can set aside a small portion of land for native plants that sustain bees all year instead of for a couple of weeks. They can also investigate organic pest control to avoid toxic chemicals. Bees are small but important contributors to the health and well-being of many species, including humans.

pages.brief: A calm nature scene with a traveling hive, a bee on a flower, tiny parasites and a peaceful safe garden sanctuary suggests the meanings of words about honeybees, their travels, health, pollination and protected habitats.

books.title: Chichén Itzá
books.art_why: This book explores the ancient Maya city and its pre-photographic history, so drawn scenes suit it.

pages.text: Location and Origin In Mexico’s Yucatan Peninsula jungle lie the ruins of Chichén Itzá, a city of massive stone structures and a network of paved roads. The city was built by the Maya, a group of people native to the area in what is now Mexico. The name Chichén Itzá means “at the mouth of the well of Itzá” in the Mayan language. The Itzá are a Maya ethnic group who lived in the northern part of the Yucatan Peninsula. The well in the name’s meaning refers to the water sources in the city, practical and sacred sites for the Maya people. A dozen or more of these statues were found at Chichén Itzá. They were used to hold offerings for the gods. Some historians date the city’s founding to the early 400s ce. Whenever it was constructed, by the 600s ce, the city was an important center for many different Maya ethnic groups. The Maya lived in Chichén Itzá for nearly one thousand years—from around 450 ce to 1450 ce. Then populations shifted away from the city, and it became mostly, but never entirely, abandoned. Since the nineteenth century, archaeologists have been studying the area of more than 7.5 square miles (19.4 sq km), with only 2 square miles (5.2 sq km) completely mapped.
pages.brief: In the jungle of Mexico’s Yucatan Peninsula lie the ruins of Chichén Itzá, with massive stone structures and a network of paved roads. The Maya built the city, and a dozen or more statues found there were used to hold offerings for the gods.

pages.text: A Maya artist created this temple carving of a jaguar, Ruler of the Underworld in Maya culture, eating a human heart. The large stepped pyramid is in the center of Chichén Itzá. Structures in Stone Today, many of the impressive buildings in Chichén Itzá have been restored to look as they would have when they were first constructed. Maya people, using stone tools, made intricate carvings on stone buildings throughout the city. From these carvings, scientists learn about the early days of the Maya culture. The most famous monument is a giant stepped pyramid, on top of which is the Temple of Kukulcán (koo-kool-KAHN), a god depicted as a winged serpent. In Maya culture, Kukulcán is the creator god, and the god of rain, wind, storms, and life. In this temple, and in many other temples in Chichén Itzá, priests led ceremonies in which gifts were offered to Maya gods.
pages.brief: A large stepped pyramid rises in the center of Chichén Itzá, topped by the Temple of Kukulcán. Nearby, a Maya stone carving shows a jaguar, Ruler of the Underworld, eating a human heart. Maya priests lead ceremonies and offer gifts to the gods in the temple.

pages.text: It is likely that one of the goals of this ancient game was to hit a ball through this ring and others like it on the field. Another of Chichén Itzá’s well-known features is the Great Ball Court, which was once home to a game called Pitz in the Mayan language. By looking at art and artifacts, scholars know that the game involved two teams of players who used their elbows, hips, and knees to hit a rubber ball. The ball was made from latex people harvested from the surrounding forests’ rubber trees. Scholars are still piecing together the rules of the game. What is known for sure is that the game was often played for fun. It also re-enacted the creation story of the Maya people, and the triumph of good over evil. Observatories are another feature of Chichén Itzá. The people of the city were dedicated to astronomy. They carefully designed several of their buildings to align with significant astronomical events, like solstices, eclipses, and lunar shifts.
pages.brief: At the Great Ball Court, two teams of Maya players use their elbows, hips, and knees to hit a rubber ball toward a stone ring. The ball is made from latex harvested from forest rubber trees. Elsewhere, Maya buildings align with the Sun, Moon, and planets for astronomy.

pages.text: Chichén Itzá Sacred Cenote Great Ball Court Venus Platform The Stepped Pyramid Temple of the Warriors The Ossuary Fresh Water Cenote El Caracol (The Snail) Casa de las Monjas (The Nunnery)
pages.brief: A wide view of Chichén Itzá in the Yucatan jungle, showing the Sacred Cenote, Great Ball Court, Venus Platform, stepped pyramid, Temple of Warriors, Ossuary, Fresh Water Cenote, El Caracol, and Casa de las Monjas among the stone structures.

pages.text: Buildings Near the Water Scholars have wondered why the Maya chose this spot to build a city. Many think they may have chosen the site based on the presence of two cenotes (say-NOH-tayz). Cenotes are spots where water wells up from beneath Earth’s surface. People used one cenote as a source of fresh water. The other, called the Sacred Cenote, had religious significance. The Maya believed that the Sacred Cenote was a pathway to the home of the rain god Chac. They believed that placing offerings in the water could win his favor and help Chac send enough rain for their crops. Archaeologists have found a number of interesting artifacts in cenotes, including tools, pottery, gold, and incense. Human bones found in the Sacred Cenote indicate that the ancient Maya sometimes carried out human sacrifice as part of their religion. Archeologists have found artifacts on the rock ledges around cenotes that were likely placed there centuries ago.
pages.brief: Two cenotes lie near Chichén Itzá, where water wells up from beneath Earth’s surface. Maya people use one for fresh water. At the Sacred Cenote, they place offerings for the rain god Chac. Tools, pottery, gold, incense, and human bones rest in the water and on rock ledges.

pages.text: A copy of a wall painting from the Temple of the Warriors shows life at a Maya waterside village with warriors in canoes. A Northern Outpost Chichén Itzá was just one of many large cities built by the Maya. Over the course of four thousand years, the Maya empire extended across land that is now five different countries— Mexico, Belize, Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador. Different Maya tribes and ethnic groups across this region spoke related languages and prayed to similar gods. They also shared a system of writing and calendars. In what archaeologists call the Preclassic (1000 bce-250 ce) and Classic (250-900 ce) periods of Maya civilization, many cities, such as Palenque (pah-LEN-keh) and Tikal (tee-KAHL) appeared in what is now southern Mexico and Guatemala.
pages.brief: A copy of a wall painting from the Temple of Warriors shows a Maya waterside village, with warriors in canoes. The scene reflects the wider Maya world across Mexico, Belize, Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador, where related languages, gods, writing, and calendars link cities such as Palenque and Tikal.

pages.text: By around the year 1000, for reasons scholars still debate, the center of the Maya world moved north to the Yucatán (yoo-kah-TAHN) Peninsula. Some experts think that war, drought, or overcrowded cities may have caused the ruin of southern Maya cities. Populations there dropped, while in the north, Chichén Itzá grew and became the most powerful city in the region. Aside from the large city of Mérida, coastal resorts, and a few other urban areas, much of the Yucatán Peninsula today is still jungles, forests, and farmland. Some Maya farmers continue to use successful farming methods passed down from their ancestors. The milpa system involves planting staple crops such as corn, beans, and squash in the same plot of land. They harvest each plant as it ripens. To replenish the soil, dead vegetation is burned, or the land is left unplanted for years. Dating back to the eleventh century, this statue shows a Chac priest. Chac is the Maya rain god, who gives or withholds rain.
pages.brief: In the Yucatán Peninsula, Chichén Itzá grows into the most powerful Maya city as southern cities decline. Around it lie jungles, forests, and farmland. Maya farmers plant corn, beans, and squash together in the milpa system, harvesting each crop as it ripens. A statue shows a Chac priest from the eleventh century.

pages.text: From One Phase to Another Over the centuries, different groups of Maya invaded and conquered Chichén Itzá. Ruling families came from elsewhere in the Yucatán as well as from the lowlands to the south and from the Gulf of Mexico. Another group, from Central Mexico, may or may not have been Maya at all. The resulting mix of cultures produced a variety of architectural styles. Many of the earlier buildings—constructed between the sixth and tenth centuries—are in the Puuc (POOK) style. The Puuc region, where the Maya city of Uxmal (oos-MAHL) was located, was west of Chichén Itzá in the Yucatán Peninsula. The Puuc style features strong horizontal lines in its design. Frequently, the lower halves of Puuc buildings are plain, while the upper halves are elaborately carved.
pages.brief: Different Maya groups invade and conquer Chichén Itzá, bringing a mix of cultures and building styles. Earlier buildings from the sixth to tenth centuries show the Puuc style: strong horizontal lines, plain lower halves, and elaborately carved upper halves. The Puuc region lies west of Chichén Itzá, where the Maya city of Uxmal stood.

pages.text: During the tenth century, Chichén Itzá was conquered by a group of outsiders who brought new architectural styles with them. Archaeologists aren’t sure whether the conquerors were the Toltec—a group of non-Maya natives from Central Mexico—or an ethnic group of Maya called the Itzá, for whom the city is named. In either case, structures that were built after this time often include both Maya and Toltec features. Many buildings, including both the stepped pyramid and the Great Ball Court, are carved with images of winged snakes and jaguars. These carvings are also seen on Toltec structures 930 miles (1497 km) to the west. The statues known as Chacmools (chahk-MOOLZ)—reclining human figures that hold offering dishes on their stomachs—may also be signs of Toltec influence. The Chacmools were used to hold offerings for the gods, such as tamales, tobacco, or flowers. Notice how the heads of all Chacmool statues are facing out.
pages.brief: After outsiders conquer Chichén Itzá in the tenth century, new buildings mix Maya and Toltec features. Winged snakes and jaguars are carved on the stepped pyramid and Great Ball Court. Chacmool statues recline with offering dishes on their stomachs, holding tamales, tobacco, or flowers, their heads all facing outward.

pages.text: Each column surrounding the Temple of Warriors has carvings of Toltec warriors. The columns were originally painted. Some paint still remains. While the people of Chichén Itzá did not maintain all the structures built in earlier styles, they didn’t necessarily demolish them, either. The Maya often chose to build a larger structure over the existing one, keeping the older building inside. Scholars think this was a way to hold onto an old temple or palace’s holiness or power, or to bring attention to history and time passing. Or it may have simply been a way to reduce the labor needed to construct an entirely new structure. In Chichén Itzá, workers built the stepped pyramid and the Temple of the Warriors on top of earlier structures.
pages.brief: Columns around the Temple of Warriors carry carvings of Toltec warriors and traces of original paint. Rather than demolish older buildings, the Maya often build larger structures over them, keeping the old temple or palace inside. At Chichén Itzá, the stepped pyramid and Temple of Warriors stand on top of earlier structures.

pages.text: Roads from the Past Maya architects didn’t restrict themselves to planning and constructing buildings. The elevated roads, or sacbeob (sahk-bay-OHB), built by the Maya are also impressive. Each sacbe (SAHK-bay) had a layer of boulders as a base, covered with increasingly fine layers of stone, gravel, and powdered limestone. At Chichén Itzá, a network of seventy to eighty sacbeob connected the buildings and cenotes. Architects constructed longer roads to connect the city to nearby communities. Centuries later, the sacbe leading to the Sacred Cenote still exists.
pages.brief: Elevated Maya roads called sacbeob connect buildings and cenotes across Chichén Itzá. Workers build each road with a base of boulders, then layers of stone, gravel, and powdered limestone. A network of seventy to eighty sacbeob links the city, and longer roads reach nearby communities. The sacbe leading to the Sacred Cenote still exists.

pages.text: Maya Calendars Haab: 365-day solar calendar divided into eighteen 20-day months and one 5-day month Tzolk’in: 260 days, which may represent nine cycles of the Moon The Calendar Round: A 52-year cycle; when each day of the Haab is matched with a day of the Tzolk’in, it takes 52 years for the same pairing to occur again. Scientific Secrets The Maya calendar systems clearly show that they had an understanding of astronomy. They invented the concept of zero, and they developed complex calendars called Haab (HAHB), Tzolk’in (ZOHL-kin), and the Calendar Round based on the movements of planets. Some Maya communities still use these calendars today. The stepped pyramid also reveals the Maya people’s understanding of astronomy. It has four staircases with ninety-one steps each. Including the platform at the top, there is a step for every day of the year. Each staircase may represent one of the four seasons. It is possible that the people of Chichén Itzá built the pyramid in a way that allowed them to use it as a calendar, helping them know when to plant and harvest crops.
pages.brief: Maya calendars include the 365-day Haab, the 260-day Tzolk’in, and the 52-year Calendar Round. The stepped pyramid has four staircases with ninety-one steps each; with the top platform, there is a step for every day of the year. Its staircases may represent four seasons, helping the Maya know when to plant and harvest.

pages.text: El Caracol (EL kah-rah- KOHL), Spanish for “the snail,” is a carefully designed round tower that is the observatory in Chichén Itzá. It provides more clues that the ancient Maya people understood the movements of the planets and stars. The building faces a different direction from any other structure in the city. Instead, it is perfectly angled for viewing Venus when it appears at its northernmost point in the sky. The small windows that remain in the ruins of El Caracol are aligned with the northernmost and southernmost positions of Venus. El Caracol was built high on a platform to rise above vegetation that could block views of the heavens. The Maya carefully planned the construction of their stepped pyramid so they could track the movement of the Sun.
pages.brief: El Caracol, Spanish for “the snail,” is a round observatory tower at Chichén Itzá. It faces a different direction from other structures, angled to view Venus at its northernmost point. Its remaining windows align with Venus’s northernmost and southernmost positions. The tower stands high on a platform to rise above vegetation, while the stepped pyramid tracks the Sun.

pages.text: The Maya Today More than six million Maya people live in Central America, including Belize, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, and Southern Mexico. They speak more than thirty languages, but their words for house, sun, time, mother, and corn sound almost identical across Mayan languages. These similarities show that some concepts are equally valued across all Maya cultures. Some of these concepts include the importance of family and community, and the relationship to corn. The Maya people continue to maintain an important connection to the sky, helping them know when to plant crops. The Maya are active participants in the international world, often integrating modern practices with ancient traditions. Maya people preserve their culture through their languages, traditions, and connections to the land and the sky. A Maya woman and children walk through a traditional marketplace in Guatemala.
pages.brief: A Maya woman and children walk through a traditional marketplace in Guatemala. More than six million Maya people live across Central America and speak more than thirty languages. Their shared words for house, sun, time, mother, and corn show valued ideas such as family, community, and corn. Maya people preserve their culture while integrating modern practices with ancient traditions.

pages.text: So many people have visited the stepped pyramid that the steps have eroded and become too dangerous to climb. A Visit to Chichén Itzá Chichén Itzá is one of the most popular sites in Mexico, and more than one million people tour the site each year. In fact, promoting tourism was a big reason the Mexican government worked to restore the site. Tourism brings money to the government and also to the local Maya communities that still surround the city. While visitors may enter many buildings, access to some structures has been restricted for the safety of the ruins as well as the visitors. Since 2006, when a tourist died in a fall down one of the steep stairways of the stepped pyramid, climbing it has been forbidden.
pages.brief: Many visitors tour Chichén Itzá each year, and the Mexican government restored the site partly to promote tourism. Tourism brings money to the government and nearby Maya communities. Some structures are restricted for safety. The stepped pyramid’s steps are eroded and too dangerous to climb, and climbing has been forbidden since a tourist died in a fall in 2006.

pages.text: At one time, an estimated fifty thousand people lived in or near Chichén Itzá. Scientists continue to learn from the treasures they left behind. The Search Continues While excavation at Chichén Itzá has revealed much, there is still a great deal to be learned. Only five years ago, archaeologists discovered jade beads, knives, animal bones, and ancient human remains in the Holtun cenote, not far from the stepped pyramid. They also found evidence that the Maya built the pyramid so that it perfectly aligns with the Sun’s path over the cenote. If Chichén Itzá’s landscape and the descendants of the Maya who built it have more to tell, people are still listening.
pages.brief: Archaeologists continue to learn from Chichén Itzá, where an estimated fifty thousand people once lived in or near the city. Recently they discovered jade beads, knives, animal bones, and ancient human remains in the Holtun cenote near the stepped pyramid. They also found evidence that the pyramid aligns with the Sun’s path over the cenote.

books.title: Genetics at Work
books.art_why: Keyword check calls for drawing; the book's concepts and historical examples are illustrated.

pages.text: Introduction What is genetics? Think about all the members of your family. Do you notice any similarities? Perhaps you all have the same hair color, or maybe many of you have long fingers or small noses. Things like hair color and body shape are traits that can be passed down to you from your grand- parents and your parents, sometimes skipping a generation or two. So when someone says you inherited your eyes from your mother, they mean your mom passed that trait down to you. Genetics is the field of science that studies how all living things pass on these traits through genes —units of heredity that determine traits in all living things. Scientists once thought that humans had about two million genes, but since the Human Genome Project began its research in the 1990s, that number has been revised to about twenty-four thousand. That’s a little more than the number of genes in a chimpanzee but not as many.
pages.brief: A family group of grandparents, parents, and a child shares similar hair color, long fingers, and small noses, with some traits skipping a generation. A scientist studies genes and chromosomes beside a chimpanzee, showing that humans have about twenty-four thousand genes, a little more than a chimpanzee.

pages.text: Family members look alike because they share the same inherited traits. as scientists first thought. Alleles are different versions of genes. Many genes have two alleles; for example, one allele of a gene will pass on brown eyes and another will pass on blue eyes. Other genes have three or more alleles; for example, the alleles for blood type are A, B, and O. Genes are made of deoxyribonucleic (dee- AHK-see-rye-bow-noo-KLAY-ik) acid ( DNA ), which is the code for your body to make the things it needs, such as enzymes for food digestion and pigment for eye color. DNA forms itself into shapes that are called chromosomes. Each cell in the human body has forty-six chromosomes—twenty-three from the mother and twenty-three from the father. It is the combination of chromosomes from both parents that makes you who you are.
pages.brief: A family group stands together with similar eyes and faces, showing shared inherited traits. Nearby, DNA strands coil into chromosome shapes, and a human cell holds forty-six chromosomes, twenty-three from the mother and twenty-three from the father. Small eye-color and blood-type examples show different alleles.

pages.text: You may be wondering what being a detective and raising dogs have to do with genetics. You will soon find out that genetics has a lot to do with these jobs and others, including farming, animal breeding, curing diseases, preventing potential illnesses, solving crimes, and more. Farming Although genetics is a new science, there is evidence of people using genetic techniques to create better crops and animals as early as 5000 BC. Many of these simple techniques are still used today. Selective breeding is one of these techniques. This technique involves scientists selecting plants with characteristics they like, such as quick- growing or attractive fruit, to breed with other plants that have those same characteristics or other desirable characteristics. By selectively breeding these plants, scientists ensure that the plants’ good traits are passed on to create crops that grow faster and produce better fruit or have other characteristics they like. Most of the foods we eat have been genetically modified, either through breeding or technology.
pages.brief: A scientist in a field selects plants with quick-growing, attractive fruit to breed with other strong plants. Nearby, a detective and a person raising dogs stand with their dogs, linking genetics to farming, animal breeding, curing diseases, preventing illness, and solving crimes.

pages.text: Think about the many types of tomatoes you can buy at the supermarket. These varieties are the result of the selective breeding of tomato plants. Some common characteristics that scientists try to propagate are faster-growing and more plentiful crops, better color and taste, durability, and resistance to disease. Wheat, soybeans, and corn are other common crops that are grown using genetic techniques. Dozens of varieties of tomatoes have been bred from a single wild variety. In the future, scientists hope to have even more control over crops. With the help of genetics, farmers will be able to grow plants for us to eat that have higher protein, lower oil, and the ability to grow faster than previous versions. Scientists also use genetic techniques with animals. For example, they use genetic breeding techniques to create chickens that lay more eggs. They produce pigs and cattle that contain meat with more or less fat, depending on how people like it. They create cows that grow faster and produce more milk. They haven’t yet figured out how to get them to produce chocolate milk, but they are probably working on it!
pages.brief: At a supermarket, many tomato varieties fill a display beside wheat, soybeans, and corn. On a farm, chickens lay eggs, pigs and cattle stand nearby, and cows are milked, showing selective breeding for better food traits and more milk.

pages.text: Genetics sounds like a great thing for farming. Why wouldn’t people want crops that grow faster and taste better, cows that produce more milk, and meat that is low in fat? Well, some say that genetically altering crops and animals will damage their genetic diversity. By only breeding for a select group of traits, many other useful traits may be lost forever. The lack of genetic diversity among crops and animals may also leave them vulnerable to a single virus that could wipe out an entire species. What happens when you crossbreed two entirely different species of animals, like a dog and an elephant? Do you get barking elephants or dogs with trunks? This type of interspecies breeding is quite complex and might seem ridiculous, but scientists are currently experi- menting with crossbreeding different species. Some people are worried that these creations might have a negative effect on the environment and on people. Selectively bred piglets grow up faster than their wild cousins.
pages.brief: Selectively bred piglets stand near wild cousins, while people look worried at a dog and an elephant placed side by side as a strange crossbreed. Crops and animals in a field suggest concern that breeding only for selected traits may damage genetic diversity.

pages.text: Not all combinations are possible, though, as most genetic crossbreeds occur within the same genus. For example, for any two species to interbreed successfully, they must have chromosomes that match up. In general, offspring from animal crossbreeding are sterile because of genetic problems in the hybrids. In plants, however, these hybrids are fertile and may produce more disease-resistant crops or flowers of rare beauty. In the future, you will probably hear a lot about this issue. People in favor of genetically altered plants and animals want to improve food productivity. Those against using genetics are concerned about the unknown effects it might have on the environment and on human health. Do You Know? Scientists have created GMOs (genetically modified organisms) by snipping individual genes from one organism and implanting them in another. Some GMOs provide food with extra nutrients, such as adding vitamin B to rice, while others create crops with built-in pesticides and preservatives. But there are concerns about GMOs. The European Union has banned GMOs until further studies are done. Many in the U.S. call for a labeling system that identifies foods containing GMOs.
pages.brief: Two animals with mismatched chromosomes stand apart, while a hybrid animal and fertile plants with rare flowers show different breeding results. A scientist snips a gene from one organism and places it into another, and rice and crops show added nutrients or built-in pest protection.

pages.text: Animal Breeding Animal breeders use some of the same genetic techniques as plant scientists, including selective breeding and hybridization. Hybridization, or crossbreeding, involves breeding different varieties or even species to combine the best characteristics of both. For example, female horses can be bred with male donkeys to produce mules. Mules are a hybrid of horses and donkeys that are tough, like donkeys, but agile, like horses. They make good work animals, but they cannot reproduce.
pages.brief: A female horse and a male donkey stand together while a sturdy mule works beside them, showing a hybrid that is tough like a donkey and agile like a horse. The mule carries a load as a work animal, with no young of its own nearby.

pages.text: Although many dog breeders raise dogs only for show, many dog breeds have been bred for specific purposes, such as hunting, herding, or guarding. Some of the earliest hunting dogs were spaniels, such as the familiar springer and cocker spaniels, which were first bred in Spain to hunt water birds like ducks or land birds like pheasants. Dog breeders determine the traits they want a dog to have and then select parents that, when bred, will pass on those traits to their offspring. Spaniels are bred in large and small versions. Today, the larger dogs are known as setters, such as the Irish setter. They earned the name setter because they “set,” or crouch, when locating wild game. Irish setters.
pages.brief: A spaniel hunts beside a pond and a field, flushing ducks from water and pheasants from grass. A larger Irish setter crouches low while locating wild game, and a breeder watches the dogs, choosing parents that will pass on wanted traits to their offspring.

pages.text: Border collies are excellent herders. The ability to herd is another desirable trait that has been bred into some dogs. Herding dogs are used to protect and round up cattle and other livestock. Border collies and Australian shepherds are popular herding dogs that have been so well bred that they continue to herd animals even if they aren’t trained to. Many people who own border collies report that their dogs attempt to herd cars and even people! The border collie breed was developed hundreds of years ago; it was originally used to herd cattle and sheep along the English-Scottish border. The Australian shepherd was developed from several herding breeds, including the border collie, which English settlers brought with them to Australia. These shepherds are still widely used in Australia, where cattle and other livestock are raised in open fields.
pages.brief: Border collies and Australian shepherds round up cattle and sheep in open fields. One collie crouches behind a car and a group of people, still trying to herd them, while a shepherd watches the dogs work the livestock.

pages.text: Some dogs have been bred as guard dogs. The Doberman pinscher and the German shepherd are two common guard dogs. Dobermans were first bred by a German watchman named Louis Dobermann in the late 1890s. The dogs have a reputation for being ferocious; however, recent breeders have worked diligently to make Dobermans a calmer, friendlier breed. German shepherds were first bred in 1899 and are descended from old breeds of herding and farm dogs. These dogs can be trained to perform many different jobs, from herding to police work to leading blind people. Many dogs are hybrids—crosses between two or more breeds, commonly called mutts. Some people believe that hybrids make the best pets because they combine the best traits of both parents. Mutts combine the best traits of many breeds.
pages.brief: A German watchman named Louis Dobermann stands with a Doberman pinscher, while a German shepherd works beside police and leads a blind person. A friendly mutt stands with two purebred dogs, showing a hybrid that combines traits from many breeds.

pages.text: Pandas have benefited from captive-breeding programs. Animals in Zoos In addition to providing education and entertainment, many zoos are also places for animal research. Genetics is an area of animal research that is performed in some zoos and is conducted to ensure that animal species survive well into the future. Genetics plays an important role in protecting many endangered and threatened animal species.
pages.brief: A panda rests in a zoo enclosure while zoo visitors watch and learn. Nearby, a zoo scientist studies other endangered animals, showing how zoos use genetics research to help animal species survive well into the future.

pages.text: One technique that zoo scientists use to increase endangered species populations is captive breeding, which is the breeding of animals that are living in captivity (such as in zoos) in order to maintain genetic diversity within a species. Some offspring bred in captivity are released into wild populations to introduce different genes that give the species a better chance of survival. This type of captive breeding is only successful if the animals can survive and reproduce on their own once they are released into the wild. Captive breeding is being used with many endangered and threatened species, including the red wolf, gorilla, panda, cheetah, and rhinoceros.
pages.brief: Zoo scientists care for a red wolf, gorilla, panda, cheetah, and rhinoceros in captivity. Some young animals are released into a wild landscape, where they must survive and reproduce on their own to add different genes to the wild population.

pages.text: Another type of captive breeding is often conducted with species that are nearly extinct and cannot survive in the wild. It gives the animals a chance to reproduce in an environment where they are protected. Although captive breeding is important, it cannot replace animals living and breeding in the wild. Zoo employees also educate people about the importance of protecting the habitats of endangered and threatened species. If wild animals such as rhinoceroses and tigers are not protected, future generations of people will only be able to read about them in books. Do You Know? Red and gray wolves are the only two species of wolves known in the world. The endangered red wolf is found in the southeastern United States. The gray wolf is found in arctic and subarctic regions around the world.
pages.brief: A rhinoceros and tiger rest in a protected zoo area while a zoo worker speaks to visitors about protecting wild habitats. In another scene, a red wolf stands in the southeastern United States and a gray wolf stands in an arctic landscape.

pages.text: Solving Crimes When crime solvers put on their detective hats these days, they have more to work with than a magnifying glass. Police, detectives, and lawyers all now use genetics and DNA to help solve crimes. All genes contain DNA—the code that determines an organism’s genetic traits. Like fingerprints, every organism’s DNA is different. A lab agent works on DNA evidence. By fingerprinting criminals, police can keep a database of fingerprints. When they find fingerprints at a crime scene, they match them with the fingerprints of known criminals in the database. Because, like fingerprints, DNA is unique, we use the term DNA fingerprinting for the use of DNA to solve crimes. The advantage of using DNA is that you do not need to find a fingerprint. Many criminals are aware that fingerprints are used to solve crimes, so they wear gloves or wipe away their fingerprints.
pages.brief: Police officers, a detective, and a lawyer examine a crime scene and DNA evidence. A lab agent works with a DNA sample, while a criminal wears gloves and wipes away fingerprints, showing why DNA can help when fingerprints are missing.

pages.text: To get a DNA fingerprint of a criminal, all you need is a small piece of skin, a single hair, or a drop of fluid such as blood or saliva. It is almost impossible for a criminal not to leave behind a trace of skin, hair, or fluid. Everywhere a person goes, he or she leaves microscopic traces of DNA. For example, if investigators find skin cells under a victim’s fingernails, they can determine the DNA of the skin cells. They then take a DNA sample from the suspect, and if the two samples match, the investigators are closer to solving the crime. Thomas McGowan (center, with his lawyers) was released from jail after being falsely imprisoned for twenty-three years. DNA evidence proved that he could not have committed the crime of which he had been accused.
pages.brief: Investigators collect a single hair, a drop of blood, and skin cells from under a victim's fingernails. A suspect provides a DNA sample for comparison. Thomas McGowan stands with his lawyers after DNA evidence proved he could not have committed the crime that kept him imprisoned for twenty-three years.

pages.text: Law enforcement agencies are now building databases of DNA samples, much as they keep collections of fingerprints. These databases contain the DNA fingerprints of convicted criminals as well as other evidence found at crime scenes. DNA has even been used to free people who were wrongly convicted of crimes. DNA fingerprinting has helped solve many crimes since it was first used in 1985. However, some people are concerned about the possible contamination affecting the accuracy of DNA testing as well as its possible misuse. Even so, DNA fingerprinting will continue to be used as long as it helps identify criminals and solve crimes. Health Genetics is used by many medical and health- care scientists. It is used to diagnose, treat, and prevent diseases as well as to develop new medicines. Medical scientists are now discovering many genes that cause specific diseases. By identifying genes that cause a specific disease, scientists can develop medicines and vaccines to cure or prevent the disease by targeting the treatments to those specific genes. Genetics counselors also use genetics to help parents and future parents figure out the odds.
pages.brief: Police build a DNA database of convicted criminals and crime-scene samples, while a freed person walks out of prison after DNA evidence cleared them. Medical scientists study disease genes and develop medicines, and a genetics counselor speaks with parents about passing on genetic disorders.

pages.text: Parents use this information to help them decide whether to have children or how to cope with the possibility of caring for children with genetic disorders. Some common genetic disorders that may be passed on from parents to their children are cystic fibrosis, Huntington’s disease, and breast cancer. Do You Know? In 2000, scientists completed the Human Genome Project, a full map of the location of every human gene. Humans have about twenty-four thousand genes arranged in a specific order on our chromosomes. It took powerful computers ten years to count and locate them all. Many diseases are caused by genes that are missing or in the wrong place.
pages.brief: Parents sit with a genetics counselor, discussing the chance of passing on disorders such as cystic fibrosis, Huntington's disease, and breast cancer. Nearby, a map of human chromosomes shows twenty-four thousand genes arranged in order, with powerful computers that took ten years to count and locate them.

pages.text: Conclusion The field of genetics offers many job opportunities. Genetics is an exciting and relatively new branch of science that brings new developments and new opportunities almost daily. Whether in plant and animal breeding, medicine, criminology, or some other field, career opportunities linked to genetics abound. Check the library or the Internet for additional information about this exciting field of science. Dolly Do You Know? The first healthy mammal ever cloned was a sheep. Cloning is the creation of an exact genetic copy of a particular living thing. The first cloned sheep, born in February 1997, was named Dolly.
pages.brief: People work in plant and animal breeding, medicine, and criminology, showing the many career opportunities in genetics. Beside them, a sheep named Dolly stands as the first healthy mammal cloned, an exact genetic copy born in February 1997.

pages.text: Explore More 1. At the Library Ask your librarian where you can find books about genetics. 2. On the Web A. In the address window, type: www.google.com. B. Then type: genetics. Click on “Google Search.” C. Read the colored links. Click on one that looks interesting. D. When you want to explore other links, click the back arrow on the top left. E. Or try some different searches: selective breeding, genetic diversity, hybridization, captive breeding, or DNA evidence. 3. In the News Genetics is still a new and controversial field of science. Check out local and national newspapers, news magazines, television, and radio for these genetics topics: A. Crimes that have been solved using DNA B. Experiments in cloning C. New medicines developed using genetics D. Controversy over genetically modified foods and animals.
pages.brief: A young reader asks a librarian for books about genetics, then sits at a computer searching for genetics topics. Nearby, newspapers, a news magazine, a television, and a radio display stories about DNA crimes, cloning experiments, new medicines, and genetically modified foods and animals.

A gardener propagates new plants over and over, and selective breeding pairs chosen plants or animals to improve their offspring.
