pages.brief: Tiny coral polyps build the Great Barrier Reef, growing on the outer skeletons of earlier polyps. Layers of skeletons form the limestone base, while algae, sponges, and shellfish add color and structure to the reef in warm tropical ocean water.

pages.text: Reefs are living organisms made out of some animals, and they supply food and shelter for other animals. They are sensitive to temperature changes in the ocean. Thousands of species live on the reef, including 1,625 kinds of fish, more than 30 kinds of marine mammals, 500 kinds of seaweed, and 6 kinds of marine turtles. The reef is also an important breeding area for animals, including birds, sea turtles, and several endangered species, such as the humpback whale, the large green sea turtle, and the dugong, or sea cow. As one of the most fascinating and beautiful places on Earth, the reef is a popular destination for groups of scientists, scuba divers, and tourists. In 1981, it was listed as a World Heritage Site by UNESCO, a division of the United Nations that focuses on education, science, and cultures of the world. Environmentalists are working with all of these groups to protect the reef so future generations can learn from it and enjoy its beauty. Additionally, multiple institutions and universities are performing research at the reef to learn how they can help protect it. Wonders Everywhere From east to west and north to south, from the highest places to the lowest, natural wonders are everywhere. Whether they formed millions.
pages.brief: A humpback whale, a large green sea turtle, and a dugong swim near the Great Barrier Reef, among many fish and marine species. The reef provides food, shelter, and breeding areas; scuba divers, scientists, and tourists visit this World Heritage Site.

pages.text: These amazing landforms are some of the most breathtaking places on Earth. Travelers, scientists, and adventure seekers will continue to visit these special places for generations to come for both study and recreation. The Grand Canyon, Paricutín, Mount Everest, Victoria Falls, and Great Barrier Reef are only five of the many wonders that surround us. Other famous natural wonders include: • The Northern Lights, or aurora borealis, a light show that brightens up the skies in the Northern Hemisphere • The Barringer Meteorite Crater, a massive hole in the Arizona desert that is almost a mile wide and 174 meters (570 ft.) deep • Ayers Rock, the world’s largest solid rock, rising 862.5 meters (2,830 ft.) above sea level in Australia • Ha Long Bay, Gulf of Tonkin, Vietnam, a large bay that contains more than 1,600 limestone islands • Eisriesenwelt (ICE-reez-on-veldt) Cave, Austria, the largest ice cave in the world, 42 kilometers (26 mi.) inside a mountain.
pages.brief: A montage-like natural scene shows the Northern Lights glowing in the Northern Hemisphere sky, Arizona's Barringer Meteorite Crater, Australia's huge Ayers Rock, Vietnam's Ha Long Bay with limestone islands, and Austria's Eisriesenwelt ice cave. These are other famous natural wonders beyond the five in the book.

books.title: Color Blindness
books.art_why: The book explains real human eyes, animals, tests, and technology that can be photographed.

pages.text: Color Blindness.
pages.brief: An opening image for a book about color blindness: a single human eye at the center of a soft spectrum that shifts from vivid colors into gray, with the surrounding space kept clean and calm. No people or scene are shown, only the eye and the fading colors.

pages.text: Choosing a red crayon is much easier for a person with full-color vision (left) than for a person with red-green color blindness (right). What Colors Do You See? Imagine looking at a box of crayons and seeing only shades of gray, blue, and yellow, or looking at a traffic signal on which the red and green lights look very similar. That’s how the world can appear to someone with color blindness. They see the world differently than people with full-color vision. Color blindness is the world’s most common genetic condition, affecting more than ten million people in the United States alone. Despite its name, though, color blindness does not cause blindness, so the medical community now calls the condition color vision deficiency (CVD). Most people affected by CVD can still see some colors. CVD simply means the inability or decreased ability to see certain colors.
pages.brief: A split scene compares two people choosing crayons from a box. On the left, a person with full-color vision picks a red crayon easily; on the right, a person with red-green color blindness sees mostly gray, blue, and yellow shades. A nearby traffic signal shows red and green lights looking very similar.

pages.text: Where Do Colors Come From? It’s easier to understand CVD when you realize that colors are actually different wavelengths of light. If you use a prism to separate white light into a rainbow, you’re actually separating the white light into its different wavelengths. The red end of the spectrum contains longer wavelengths of light while shorter wavelengths of light are at the purple end. Objects appear to be different colors because they absorb and reflect different wavelengths of light. For example, a ripe strawberry looks red because it reflects long (red) wavelengths. If it instead reflected short wavelengths of light, it would look blue! The flower’s petals look red because they reflect long (red) wavelengths, while its leaves look green because they reflect medium (green) wavelengths.
pages.brief: A prism stands on a surface, splitting a beam of white light into a rainbow. The red end of the spectrum stretches into longer wavelengths, while the purple end shows shorter wavelengths. Nearby, a ripe strawberry reflects red light, and a flower with red petals and green leaves shows how objects reflect different wavelengths.

pages.text: How an Eye Sees rods cones How Color Vision Works Humans see colors because light-detecting cells in our eyes respond differently to different wavelengths of light. When light enters one of your eyes, the lens focuses it on the retina, a thin layer of tissue at the back of the eyeball. There it activates light-sensitive cells, called rod cells and cone cells. Activated cells send electrical signals to the brain through the optic nerve, where they are translated into images.
pages.brief: A cutaway view of a human eye shows light entering through the lens and focusing on the retina at the back. There, rod cells and cone cells become active and send electrical signals along the optic nerve toward the brain, where the signals are translated into images. The eye’s internal structures are visible in clear detail.

pages.text: Rods and Cones Rod cells are the most sensitive cells in your retina. They allow you to see in extremely dim light, but they can’t tell different colors apart. Cone cells are responsible for color vision. Each cell contains one of three different light-absorbing molecules, called photopigments, which detect blue, green, or red light. Combining these three main colors allows you to see thousands of colors. When one or more photopigments aren’t functioning properly, though, CVD ensues. honeybee vision human vision Color Vision in Animals Most animals can see fewer colors than humans. For instance, dogs can only see shades of blue and yellow; bulls cannot see the color red; and other animals—including some birds, bees, and butterflies—see more colors than humans do, including ultraviolet and infrared wavelengths of light that are invisible to humans. Animals use the information they gather from colors around them to communicate with each other, hunt prey for food, and defend themselves from predators.
pages.brief: Rod cells and cone cells appear inside the retina, with rods suited to dim light and cones detecting blue, green, or red light. Beside them, a honeybee and a human eye suggest different color vision. Across the scene, a dog, a bull, a bird, a bee, and a butterfly stand as examples of animals that see fewer or more colors.

pages.text: Different Types of CVD Red-Green CVD Red-green CVD, which causes difficulty when it comes to telling the difference between red and green, is the most common type of color vision condition. It’s hereditary, found most often in Caucasian people of northern European ancestry. It’s also more common in men, of which it affects one out of twelve, than in women, of which it affects only one in two hundred. Red-green CVD is usually caused by defects in the green photopigment. Without the green photopigment, green and yellow objects appear reddish in color. Defects in the red photopigment also cause red-green CVD. In this case, red, orange, and yellow objects appear green or black. Although people with red-green CVD have difficulty distinguishing colors, they can still see clearly because red and green cones have some overlap in the wavelengths of light they detect. Their eyes can still detect incoming light even if one type of cone is missing or malfunctioning. full-color vision red yellow green red-green CVD vision red yellow green.
pages.brief: A side-by-side comparison shows red, yellow, and green objects as seen with full-color vision and with red-green CVD. In the first view the colors are distinct; in the second they shift toward similar reddish or greenish tones. A man and a woman nearby represent the different rates at which red-green CVD affects men and women.

pages.text: CVD Blue-Yellow CVD Blue-yellow CVD occurs when the blue photopigment is malfunctioning or is missing. It’s fairly rare, only occurring in about one out of every ten thousand people worldwide and, unlike red-green CVD, it’s equally common in men and women. Some people with blue-yellow CVD have no blue cone cells at all, which causes them to see blue as green and to see yellow as violet or gray. More commonly, people who have blue-yellow CVD have partially functional blue cone cells and, as a result, have difficulty distinguishing yellow and red from pink. full-color vision blue-yellow CVD.
pages.brief: A comparison of full-color vision and blue-yellow CVD shows blue, yellow, red, pink, and green objects under each condition. In the blue-yellow view, blue may appear green and yellow may look violet or gray, while yellow and red are harder to tell from pink. The scene stays calm and clear so the color differences are easy to notice.

pages.text: Complete CVD Complete CVD is the most severe form of CVD. This condition occurs when there are defects in two or more of the three types of cones. You might think that a single kind of cone would be enough to enable color vision, but you’d be mistaken. The brain must compare color information from at least two distinct types of cone cells to identify colors. That means people who have only blue cone cells, for example, are able to see blue wavelengths of light, but they can’t distinguish any colors. Some traffic lights use shapes as well as colors to convey information to drivers with CVD. People who are missing two or more types of cones tend to be particularly sensitive to light and may also have difficulty seeing clearly, especially in bright light. That’s because they have to rely on rod cells for most or all of their vision, and rod cells only function in dim lighting conditions. Only about one out of thirty thousand people worldwide are missing all three types of cones. People who lack any functioning cone cells see the world in shades of black, white, and gray.
pages.brief: A person with complete CVD stands in bright light, shading their eyes, while nearby objects appear in shades of black, white, and gray. A traffic signal uses different shapes as well as colors to help drivers understand it. The person’s sensitive eyes and reduced color vision are the focus of the scene.

pages.text: The Challenges of CVD People with CVD may face some challenges. For example, they may have trouble reading color- coded information on maps, graphs, and charts. Children with CVD may have challenges with classwork, especially if their CVD has not been diagnosed. Red-green CVD makes it difficult to read yellow chalk on a green chalkboard, and all types of CVD make it difficult to choose the correct colors for art and science projects. CVD can also cause safety issues. Fire hydrants, car warning lights, and emergency equipment are often colored red or yellow to make them more visible. These bright colors may be obvious to those with full-color vision but unnoticeable to those with CVD. People with this condition may also have difficulty noticing sunburns, rashes, or undercooked meat. In some cases, CVD may be a factor when a person chooses what career to pursue. Some positions, such as geologist or commercial airline pilot, require full-color vision. Other careers, such as interior designer, photographer, and food inspector, are significantly more challenging without full-color vision. Still, people with CVD can usually work around those challenges to succeed at almost any job.
pages.brief: A child with CVD works at a desk with a color-coded map, graph, and chart, looking unsure. Behind them, yellow chalk stands out weakly on a green chalkboard. Nearby are a red fire hydrant and car warning lights, plus examples of art and science projects where choosing colors is difficult. The scene suggests everyday challenges and safety concerns.

pages.text: Testing for CVD The Ishihara Test is the most common test for red-green color vision conditions. It uses images composed of dots that are different sizes and colors. People with full-color vision can see numbers or shapes inside the picture, but people with red-green CVD may find it difficult or impossible to identify the hidden symbols. Other, similar tests are used to detect yellow- blue CVD. Can you see the hidden numbers or shapes in the circles in this Ishihara Test?
pages.brief: Several circular patterns made of dots in different sizes and colors fill the page, like a color vision test. Inside some circles, hidden numbers or shapes are easy to see with full-color vision; others are difficult or impossible to find for a person with red-green CVD. The dot patterns are shown clearly and evenly.

pages.text: These special sunglasses from EnChroma allow people with red-green CVD to see a much more colorful world when they wear them. Tools to Help People with CVD Currently, there’s no known cure for CVD, but modern technology has led to the development of many new tools to help people with this condition. Smartphone apps can perform helpful tasks, such as identifying colors and recommending complementary colors. These apps can even help people choose matching clothes or tell which fruits are ripe at the grocery store. Some smartphone apps can only identify colors after the user snaps a photo. Others can analyze the colors in the camera’s viewfinder without requiring the user to take a photo first, which allows users to identify colors in real time. Researchers have also created high-tech tinted lenses that filter out specific wavelengths of light. Special sunglasses that use these lenses allow people with red-green CVD to distinguish between the two colors.
pages.brief: Special tinted sunglasses rest beside a smartphone held up toward clothing and ripe fruit. On the phone’s screen, colors in the camera view are analyzed in real time, helping a person with red-green CVD choose matching clothes and judge which fruit is ripe. The sunglasses filter specific wavelengths so red and green become easier to tell apart.

pages.text: Treating CVD Although no true treatment for CVD currently exists, that may soon change because scientists were able to find a workaround for red-green CVD in squirrel monkeys recently. The monkeys lacked the red photopigment and, as a result, couldn’t tell the difference between red and green. Researchers used a technology called gene therapy to change traits in the monkeys. They engineered a specially constructed virus to insert the red photopigment gene into the monkeys’ green cone cells. Within about twenty weeks, treated monkeys could distinguish between red and green dots. A squirrel monkey takes a color test. This was exciting news because the monkeys had lived with CVD since birth. Many doctors and scientists had predicted that it would be impossible for them to see in full color because their brains would not have developed the connections needed to interpret color information, connections that usually develop when animals are young. Now that we know that there is a work-around for CVD in adult squirrel monkeys, there’s hope for people who may want to have full-color vision, too.
pages.brief: A squirrel monkey sits before red and green dots in a color test while researchers watch. The scene recalls the gene therapy work: a specially constructed virus carried the red photopigment gene into green cone cells, and within about twenty weeks treated monkeys could distinguish red from green. The monkey’s eyes and the testing setup are the focus.

pages.text: Living with CVD CVD is a fairly common condition that can be inherited by anyone. Perhaps you or someone in your family has CVD or knows someone who does. Detecting CVD early can help people understand and adjust to what they are seeing. Though CVD adds some challenge to certain activities, most people with CVD get along just fine. They may see the world a little bit differently, but that doesn’t stop them from having rich, fulfilling lives.
pages.brief: A family group stands together in a bright, everyday setting, including one person with CVD who is going about life confidently. Around them are simple signs of school, work, and home activities, suggesting that early detection helps people understand and adjust to what they see. The mood is calm and hopeful, not limited by the condition.

pages.text: (n.) page 8 family members and relations from past times complementary (adj.) page 13 serving to complete, balance, or improve something else cone cells (n.) page 6 cells in the eye’s retina that are color sensitive and work best in bright light defects (n.) page 8 weaknesses, imperfections, or failures genetic condition (n.) page 4 an inherited physical condition that is caused by a problem in one or more genes hereditary (adj.) page 8 of or relating to genetic traits passed from parents to offspring Glossary molecules (n.) page 7 the smallest parts of substances that can exist by themselves, made of one or more atoms photopigments (n.) page 7 natural compounds that undergo chemical changes when they absorb light prism (n.) page 5 a clear object that bends light so that it separates into a rainbow of colors retina (n.) page 6 tissue at the back of the eye that receives images and transmits them to the brain rod cells (n.) page 6 cells in the eye’s retina that are light sensitive and work best in dim light wavelengths (n.) page 5 the distances between the consecutive high or low points of a wave.
pages.brief: A collection of small illustrations for a glossary page: a prism splitting light into a rainbow, an eye showing the retina and cone cells, rod cells in dim light, a family group for ancestry, simple molecules and photopigments, and objects that look complementary. Each image is separate and clearly arranged.

books.title: Stonehenge
books.art_why: Prehistoric construction predates photography, and this is not a named-person biography.

pages.text: Stonehenge is one of the most popular prehistoric sites in the world. Stonehenge is one of the most popular prehistoric sites in the world. A Monument from Before Written History Thousands of years ago, a community of people went to great effort to raise a ring of massive stones in southern England. Today, this monument is known as Stonehenge. As the centuries have passed, many of these huge megaliths have fallen over. Still, it has remained a place of fascination long after people forgot its original purpose. About nine hundred years ago, an English historian, Geoffrey of Monmouth, tried to explain the mysterious monument. He told a fanciful story about Merlin, the mythical wizard of the King Arthur legends. He wrote that Merlin advised another king to create a memorial that would stand forever. The result was Stonehenge. Monmouth claimed it was built with the aid of Merlin’s magic about sixteen hundred years ago.
pages.brief: A ring of massive stones stands and leans on a grassy plain in southern England, with several megaliths fallen. In an imagined scene, an English historian writes about Merlin, a mythical wizard, advising a king to create a memorial that would stand forever.

pages.text: For hundreds of years, archaeologists, historians, and scientists have been investigating Stonehenge, seeking scientific explanations instead of supernatural ones. Archaeologists have excavated the site for clues about its history, builders, and purpose. What researchers have learned is just as remarkable as any legend of kings, wizards, and magic. Scholars once believed Stonehenge was approximately two thousand years old, but they were stunned when research revealed its builders had begun work on it three thousand years before that. This was during the Neolithic period (10,000–2500 bc), a time before the people in Britain had developed metalworking or even invented the wheel. Archaeologists investigate the origin of the bluestones, a rare type of stone used at Stonehenge. Archaeologists investigate the origin of the bluestones, a rare type of stone used at Stonehenge.
pages.brief: Archaeologists work in excavated trenches at Stonehenge, examining soil and rare bluestones for clues. Researchers study the ancient site on a grassy plain, considering a Neolithic world without metalworking or the wheel, long before scholars once believed the monument was built.

pages.text: United Kingdom SCOTLAND NORTHERN IRELAND ENGLAND IRELAND Stone Age Site Stonehenge is built of earth and huge rocks. It is not towering like the Washington Monument or enormous like the great pyramids of Egypt. Instead, it owes much of its majesty to the mystery of its ancient origins. As visitors approach Stonehenge, located on a grassy plain in southern England, its massive standing stones gradually come into view. The monument consists of circles built inside circles. The outer ring is a ditch that surrounds an embankment of raised soil measuring about 110 meters (360 ft.) in diameter. In the center stands the famous ring of stones, many of which are now missing.
pages.brief: On a grassy plain in southern England, visitors approach Stonehenge as massive standing stones come into view. The monument shows circles within circles: an outer ditch and raised earth embankment surround a central ring of stones, many now missing, not towering like a pyramid or monument.

pages.text: Different kinds of stones are used at Stonehenge. The standing sandstone slabs that form the outer ring are called sarsen stones, the largest of which weighs about 36,000 kilograms (79,366 lb.). Stone lintels lie across the tops of the standing stones and once connected all of them together. Smaller boulders called bluestones lie within the sarsen circle. They are made of a type of rock called dolerite, a coarse basalt rock. The largest bluestone weighs about 2,994 kilograms (6,600 lb.). Inside the ring of sarsen stones is another group of standing stones, set in a horseshoe shape. These stones form trilithons, square arches with two standing stones and one lintel lying across. They measure approximately 6.7 meters (22 ft.) across and 9 meters (29.5 ft.) tall. An artist shows what Stonehenge might have looked like when it was complete.
pages.brief: A cutaway view shows Stonehenge’s different stones: huge sandstone sarsen slabs forming an outer ring, stone lintels resting across their tops, and smaller bluestones inside. Within the sarsen circle, a horseshoe of trilithons—two standing stones with one lintel—stands tall, as an artist imagines the monument complete.

pages.text: Stonehenge lintel sarsen stone • Today, seventeen sarsen stones mark the curve of the Sarsen Circle, but archaeologists believe there were thirty at one time. • The large blocks average 22,680 kilograms (50,000 lb.)— more than a school bus—and stand more than 5 meters (16.4 ft.) tall. • Free-standing stones, including the Heel Stone and Slaughter Stone, are part of the monument but lie outside of the Sarsen Circle. • Some stones may have been dragged off over the last few thousand years, and others likely sank into the ground. • Important rituals were likely staged at Stonehenge—crowning rulers, celebrating harvests, or honoring dead ancestors. Some experts believe only high priests or other religious leaders were allowed inside the sacred circle of stones. trilithon bluestones.
pages.brief: Seventeen sarsen stones curve along the Sarsen Circle, though archaeologists believe thirty once stood. Each huge block weighs more than a school bus and stands over five meters tall. Outside the circle lie free-standing stones, the Heel Stone and Slaughter Stone. Inside, experts imagine high priests or religious leaders staging rituals such as crowning rulers or honoring ancestors.

pages.text: A Landscape of Monuments Stonehenge sits on Salisbury Plain, an area of rolling hills and grasslands. Evidence suggests people have been living there for more than ten thousand years. During the Neolithic period, Salisbury Plain was wooded and filled with animal life. It was a place of plenty for people who lived as hunter-gatherers. Archaeologists have unearthed ancient pits containing flint tools and weapons along with animal bones. Experts speculate these Neolithic people may have considered the area sacred because of the abundance of food. Gradually, beginning around 7500 bc, a culture- shaking change took place. The people inhabiting the area began slowly shifting from hunting and gathering to farming. Agriculture made it possible to produce food more reliably and feed larger groups of people. Farming also made large social projects possible. With sufficient food supplies, people there could spend less time farming and hunting and had more time to work on monuments like Stonehenge. Sheep graze on the lush grass of Salisbury Plain near Stonehenge. Sheep graze on the lush grass of Salisbury Plain near Stonehenge.
pages.brief: Sheep graze on the lush grass of Salisbury Plain, a landscape of rolling hills near Stonehenge. In Neolithic times the plain was wooded and full of animals, where hunter-gatherers left flint tools and bones in pits. Later people slowly shifted to farming, producing reliable food and gaining time to build monuments.

pages.text: A Project of 1,500 Years Archaeological evidence indicates the construction of Stonehenge began around 3000 bc. Amazingly, generations of people continued to work on it for more than a thousand years. Experts view the transport and placement of the giant stones as one of the great engineering feats of early human history. Archaeologists believe the builders brought the sarsen stones from distant quarries located about 32 to 48 kilometers (20–30 mi.) away. How were these giant stones hauled so far in a time before wheels and wagons? That question has led to far-fetched theories about giants, magic, and even space aliens. Archaeologists have focused on more realistic options. Teams of researchers have conducted experiments, trying to figure out how Stone Age technology could have been used to move the sarsen stones. Researchers have loaded replica stones of similar weights onto wooden sledges. They then slid these sled-like platforms along wooden rails greased with animal fat, pulled by dozens of volunteers. These trials proved it possible to move the giant stones to the Stonehenge site, and this has become a leading theory of how it was done.
pages.brief: Teams of volunteers pull replica sarsen stones loaded on wooden sledges along greased wooden rails, testing how Stone Age people moved giant stones without wheels or wagons. The experiment suggests builders could haul sarsen stones from distant quarries, about thirty-two to forty-eight kilometers away, to the Stonehenge site.

pages.text: For many years, the bluestones presented a greater mystery since no source for them is found anywhere near Stonehenge. Eventually, investigations led researchers to a quarry in Wales—more than 241 kilometers (150 mi.) to the north. For some unknown reason, the creators of Stonehenge believed the heavy bluestones were important enough to transport staggering distances. Some experts speculate these stones may have been loaded onto rafts that floated along the ocean coast to bring them nearer to the Stonehenge site. These volunteers conducted an experiment in London in May 2016 to see if people could pull a heavy block of stone, such as the ones used at Stonehenge, without the use of machinery.
pages.brief: Volunteers in London pull a heavy stone block with ropes, testing whether people could move Stonehenge-sized stones without machinery. The bluestones’ source was a mystery until researchers traced them to a quarry in Wales, more than 241 kilometers north. Some experts wonder if rafts carried them along the ocean coast.

pages.text: Raising the standing stones presented a different engineering challenge. One possible method involved digging a pit under the base of each long slab of stone. Then, wooden wedges could have been inserted gradually beneath the top end, raising it little by little. Once the top was high enough, the bottom then dropped into the pit, and finally, people used ropes to pull it into vertical position. Some researchers believe the builders of Stonehenge raised stones by erecting wooden platforms beneath them. Placing the lintels on top of the trilithons may have required the most planning and expertise. One possibility is that the builders constructed ramps of dirt and wood that reached to the tops of each pair of standing stones. The lintel might then have been mounted on a sledge, where teams of workers would have used ropes to carefully slide it up the ramp and into place.
pages.brief: Builders raise a long standing stone by digging a pit beneath its base, then easing wooden wedges under the top to tilt it upward. Ropes pull it vertical as the bottom drops into place. For lintels, workers might slide a stone on a sledge up a dirt-and-wood ramp to the trilithon tops.

pages.text: Who were these master builders who developed such innovative engineering techniques? It is nearly impossible to know what languages they spoke or which religions they practiced. They did not use writing and left behind few examples of their art. All modern understanding of them must be gleaned from archaeological evidence. Testing of human skeletons and animal bones found near the site offer fascinating clues about their origins. Some of the people who built Stonehenge seem to have moved there from Wales and other neighboring lands. Archaeologists excavate a quarry in Pembrokeshire, Wales, where Stonehenge’s bluestones possibly originated.
pages.brief: Archaeologists excavate a quarry in Pembrokeshire, Wales, where Stonehenge’s bluestones may have originated. Nearby, researchers study human skeletons and animal bones for clues about the master builders, who left no writing and little art. Evidence suggests some builders moved to the area from Wales and neighboring lands.

pages.text: However, recent discoveries indicate that a few migrated from as far away as mainland Europe. The grand scale of Stonehenge suggests different groups banded together and shared their knowledge, skills, and muscle to create it. The Amesbury Archer In 2002, archaeologists discovered a skeleton near Amesbury, a town about 3.2 kilometers (2 mi.) from Stonehenge. He died about 4,300 years ago, during the time Stonehenge was still being built. He must have been important because his grave contained gold jewelry, arrowheads, and stone wrist guards commonly worn by archers at that time. By testing chemicals in his teeth, researchers found evidence that he grew up in mainland Europe, near where Germany and Switzerland are today. For some yet unknown reason, this man migrated more than 1,126 kilometers (700 mi.). He died far from his homeland and was buried with honor. Earrings, rings, pots, and a knife are some of the many objects found surrounding the Amesbury Archer’s skeleton. Earrings, rings, pots, and a knife are some of the many objects found surrounding the Amesbury Archer’s skeleton.
pages.brief: Beside a skeleton found near Amesbury, objects include gold earrings, rings, pots, a knife, arrowheads, and stone wrist guards. The Amesbury Archer, who died about 4,300 years ago while Stonehenge was being built, grew up in mainland Europe near Germany and Switzerland, then migrated far and was buried with honor.

pages.text: Pondering the Purpose of Stonehenge As mysterious as Stonehenge is, clues about its purpose exist in its design. It does not seem to have ever served any practical purpose, like a shelter or market. For this reason, experts are convinced Stonehenge was an open-air temple, a place people visited for spiritual reasons. Researchers believe its religious and ceremonial purposes changed over the course of its long history. Stonehenge likely began as a burial site. Archaeologists have unearthed as many as 240 burials near the monument, making it the largest Neolithic cemetery in England. Many of the bodies were cremated, and some remains were buried with weapons and jewelry. A Neolithic man’s skeleton found at Stonehenge, along with his reconstructed face, are on display at the visitor center near Stonehenge.
pages.brief: A Neolithic man’s skeleton and his reconstructed face are displayed at the visitor center near Stonehenge. Around the monument, archaeologists have unearthed as many as 240 burials, some cremated and some with weapons and jewelry, making it England’s largest Neolithic cemetery. Experts think Stonehenge served as an open-air temple and burial site.

pages.text: Another popular theory about Stonehenge involves astronomy, since some of the giant stones align with the movements of the sun. This is particularly apparent during the summer and winter solstices. The summer solstice, on about June 21 each year, marks the longest day of the year. At dawn that morning, the sun’s rays reach directly to the monument’s center. The winter solstice, which occurs about December 22, marks the shortest day of the year. At sunset, the sun shines directly between the largest pair of sarsen stones. In a sense, the arrangement of the monument’s stones functions like a giant clock marking the passing of the seasons. For a farming culture, this was vital information for planning when to plant crops. In recent years, another theory has emerged about the purpose of Stonehenge. Some experts believe it might have been a huge community project to unite people in the area. Evidence suggests that tribes from far and wide journeyed to Stonehenge and many settled there permanently. Perhaps they came to trade or band together for protection, or they could have been drawn by an abundance of food in the region.
pages.brief: At dawn on the summer solstice, sunlight reaches directly to Stonehenge’s center; at sunset on the winter solstice, it shines between the largest pair of sarsen stones. The stones act like a giant seasonal clock. Experts also wonder whether tribes journeyed there to trade, find protection, share food, and unite in a huge community project.

pages.text: The sun rises, shining through the stones of Stonehenge on June 21, 2014, the longest day of the year. Stonehenge Today Stonehenge is one of the most famous prehistoric landmarks in Europe. The Stonehenge the public sees today is not what people saw in 1900. By then, most of the giant stones had tilted or toppled. But in the last century, heritage groups have restored parts of the monument based on archaeological evidence. In 1958, cranes were used to lift some of the stones, and some of the standing stones were anchored in concrete. The restorers believed these restorations would give the public a better idea of the monument’s original appearance. Observers watch as the largest crane in England is used to place a lintel across two of Stonehenge’s standing stones in 1958.
pages.brief: Observers watch England’s largest crane lift a lintel into place across two standing stones at Stonehenge in 1958. Restorers used cranes and concrete to anchor tilted or toppled stones, hoping to show the monument’s original appearance. On June 21, 2014, the summer solstice sun rises shining through the stones.

pages.text: Researchers continue to investigate Stonehenge and the surrounding area. Today, they use the latest technology to help them map what is hidden beneath their feet. This equipment includes magnetometers that detect magnetic fields, laser scanners that measure potential archaeological sites precisely, and ground- penetrating radar that can scan as deep as 9 meters (29.5 ft.) underground. Tourists can visit Stonehenge’s visitor center and interact with its exhibits. Replicas of Neolithic houses have been created using authentic materials and techniques, such as roof thatching, based on archaeological finds in the area. Volunteers demonstrate ancient rope weaving, pottery making, and grain grinding. More than nine hundred thousand people visit Stonehenge a year, including two children who try to pull a sarsen stone (left). Visitors go inside reconstructed Neolithic huts like those in which the builders of Stonehenge might have lived (right).
pages.brief: Two children try to pull a sarsen stone at Stonehenge, while visitors step inside reconstructed Neolithic huts with thatched roofs. In the visitor center, exhibits and volunteers demonstrate ancient rope weaving, pottery making, and grain grinding. Researchers nearby use magnetometers, laser scanners, and ground-penetrating radar to map what lies hidden underground.

pages.text: The Story of Stonehenge Continues Stonehenge is an amazing landmark of an ancient time and place. Visitors marvel at the ingenuity of those who designed the monument to align with the sun’s movements. Impressed by its massive stones, they can picture hundreds of people working together to transport them to the site. They may wonder at the kind of teamwork and muscle it must have required to raise the heavy stones and link them together. For centuries, Stonehenge served as a central sacred site for the people who lived in the lands around it. The United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) named Stonehenge a World Heritage Site worthy of special recognition and protection. Today, it stirs the imaginations of people all around the world. Stonehenge is not the only stone circle in England. A larger stone circle has been found in Avebury, 40 kilometers (25 mi.) north of Stonehenge.
pages.brief: Visitors marvel at Stonehenge’s massive stones and imagine hundreds of people working together to transport and raise them. For centuries the site served as a central sacred place for surrounding communities. UNESCO named it a World Heritage Site, and a larger stone circle at Avebury lies forty kilometers north.

books.title: Argentina
books.art_why: The book spans the 1500s invasion, the 1816 congress and the 1800s Golden Age, so drawn scenes are needed.

pages.text: Argentina PARAGUAY BOLIVIA BRAZIL CHILE Buenos Aires PACIFIC OCEAN URUGUAY ARGENTINA ATLANTIC OCEAN Where Is It? Argentina is the second-largest country on the continent of South America and the eighth-largest country in the world. Its land covers 2,736,690 square kilometers (1,056,642 sq. mi.) and lies between the Andes Mountains, the longest mountain chain on Earth, and the Atlantic Ocean. The countries of Brazil, Uruguay, Paraguay, Bolivia, and Chile border Argentina. Twenty-three provinces make up Argentina. Each one has an independent government with its own laws and constitution. However, every province must follow and answer to the laws of Argentina’s national government.
pages.brief: A wide view of the South American continent from above. Argentina's long, tapering triangle fills the south, the jagged Andes ridge running the whole length of its western edge, the Atlantic Ocean breaking along its eastern shore, and greener neighbouring lands pressing in from the north. The capital's buildings cluster near a wide river mouth.

pages.text: The capital and largest city in Argentina is Buenos Aires, whose name means “fair or good winds.” Its population is more than fifteen million people. The city boasts the widest street in the world. People named Avenida 9 de Julio (July 9th Avenue) for the date of Argentina’s independence from the country of Spain. Buenos Aires is one of the largest ports in South America. The city is the center of many economic activities, including the nation’s banking, food processing, and automobile industries. Known for the friendliness of its residents, Buenos Aires is a multicultural city and home to diverse groups of people. It has one of the largest middle classes in Latin America. Many of the people who live and work there enjoy city life and all it has to offer. Buenos Aires looks quite a bit like a European city due to the traditions brought there by many of its residents. The obelisk on Avenida 9 de Julio was built in 1936. It honors the four hundredth birthday of Buenos Aires.
pages.brief: Avenida 9 de Julio in Buenos Aires, the widest street in the world, with lanes of traffic and pedestrians crossing beneath a tall white obelisk. Banks, food-processing plants and car factories stand around it, along with European-style buildings and balconies. Residents stroll and chat on the busy pavements near the port.

pages.text: More than forty-three million people live in Argentina, with more than 90 percent of the population living in its four largest cities. Argentina has the third-largest economy in Latin America, after Brazil and Mexico. Argentina is strong in agriculture and rich with natural resources such as silver, gold, oil, and natural gas. Its exports include wine and beef as well as lemons, grapes, peanuts, tea, and wheat. Most Argentines work in service jobs, but work is also available in the country’s automobile, textile, energy, communications, and appliance industries. Argentina also offers employment in the film industry, with dozens of motion pictures produced there every year. Argentina has a strong agricultural history. Farmers harvest wheat (left) and grapes (below). People.
pages.brief: Farmers in a golden wheat field cut stalks and load them onto a cart, while nearby workers pick bunches of grapes in a vineyard, filling baskets. Beyond the fields stand oil and gas machinery and factories making cars, textiles and appliances, with a film crew shooting a scene at the edge of a town.

pages.text: The Roman Catholic faith is Argentina’s official religion. However, the country guarantees freedom of religion, and people also practice the Muslim, Jewish, Protestant, and Mormon religions. Like many countries, Argentina can be considered a “melting pot” because diverse peoples came together from all over the world to form a new nation. Argentina has always welcomed new immigrants. Today, the majority of Argentines have European roots. Argentina’s official language is Spanish. However, since most Argentines trace their roots back to Europe, some people also speak other languages, including Italian, German, French, and English. Visitors will notice European architecture in Villa General Belgrano, a district in the province of Córdoba.
pages.brief: In Villa General Belgrano, a district of Córdoba province, half-timbered European-style buildings with steep roofs and shuttered windows line a tidy street. Families of European descent and newer immigrants walk together, some pausing by a small church, others chatting outside shops. Trees shade the pavements and flower boxes hang from balconies.

pages.text: Argentina’s Five Regions Land Shaped like a long triangle, Argentina has mountains, deserts, plains, glaciers, vast lakes, and seashores. Five major regions make up Argentina’s varied land. The Andes Mountains form a great wall between Chile and Argentina. The Pampas region is a large area of flat, fertile land where people grow many crops. Patagonia—the largest region and home to the oil and gas industries— is known for its ecotourism. The Littoral region, in the north, has jungles and swamps, while the Gran Chaco region is a lowland in the northwest. PACIFIC OCEAN ATLANTIC OCEAN The countries of Brazil and Paraguay meet Argentina in an area called the Triple Frontier, which is formed by the Iguazú and Paraná Rivers. Here, the Iguazú River tumbles over horseshoe- shaped falls that extend 2.7 kilometers (1.7 mi.).
pages.brief: A wide view of Argentina's five regions: the Andes standing as a great wall in the west, flat fertile Pampas farmland in the centre, Patagonia's dry open country to the south, the jungles and swamps of the Littoral in the north, and the low Gran Chaco plain in the northwest, where the Iguazú River tumbles over a horseshoe of falls.

pages.text: Iguazú Falls are taller and wider than most of the waterfalls in the world. They formed millions of years ago when a volcanic eruption left a huge crack in the earth. The name of the falls comes from a language of native people in the region and means “big water.” With its many habitats, Argentina is alive with different kinds of birds and mammals. Toucans, Andean condors, penguins, pumas, tapirs, howler monkeys, and jaguars are all residents. Mount Aconcagua, in the Andes, is the highest mountain peak in the Americas. Iguazú Falls are one of the seven natural wonders of the world. The towering Andes Mountains, stretching the full length of western South America, are one of Earth’s great natural features. The Andes range is about 7,242 kilometers (4,500 mi.) long and runs through seven countries. Its highest peak— Mount Aconcagua—is 6,962 meters (22,841 ft.) tall.
pages.brief: Iguazú Falls thunders over a horseshoe ledge in the jungle, mist rising from the water. Toucans, howler monkeys and a jaguar perch in the surrounding trees, a penguin stands on a southern shore and a condor circles overhead. Far west, the long wall of the Andes rises, its highest peak, Mount Aconcagua, capped with snow.

pages.text: History Argentina has had a long and troubled history. Native peoples have lived here for thousands of years, but many died from disease and warfare following the Spanish invasion in the 1500s. After Argentina declared its independence from Spain in 1816, Spanish rule was finally banished in the country. The Argentine Republic was founded in 1853, and Buenos Aires became its official capital in 1880. Some people call the years from 1880 to 1914 the “Golden Age” of Argentina. Railroads expanded, sheep farming and cattle ranching became very important, and roads, buildings, and parks were built. However, with the Great Depression in 1929, Argentina’s economy struggled and military dictators rose to power. Dictatorships ruled from 1929 until 1943, when another military leader, Juan Perón, helped overthrow the government. A painting shows the congress that declared Argentina free from Spain in 1816.
pages.brief: A painted scene of the congress of 1816, men in dark coats declaring Argentina free from Spain inside a colonial hall. Around it, scenes from the country's past: native peoples, Spanish invaders, a railway engine pushing across the plains, cattle and sheep grazing, and new roads, buildings and parks rising in a growing town.

pages.text: In 1946, Juan Perón was elected president. Perón’s popularity increased as he introduced reforms such as health services and retirement money for the majority of Argentines. Although he and his wife, Eva, introduced these good things to the working classes, Perón also ignored human rights and acted like a dictator. His popularity weakened during his second term as president, and he fled Argentina for Spain in 1955. Juan and Eva Perón However, Perón returned to Argentina in 1973. He ran for president once again and won a decisive victory. He died the following year. While the Peróns have critics, today many Argentines remember them as good leaders who helped the working classes and modernized Argentina. During the decades following Perón’s rule, Argentina experienced more military takeovers and economic turmoil. However, since 1983, democracy has taken hold, the economy has grown, and millions of new jobs have been created. Even with its rocky past, Argentina seems to have a promising future.
pages.brief: Juan and Eva Perón stand together on a balcony, he in uniform, she in an elegant dress, waving to a crowd of working people packed into the square below. Behind them the government building's columns glow in the sun, while elsewhere Argentines queue at a new health clinic and collect retirement money.

pages.text: Celebrations Modern Argentina comes alive with its yearly festivals. Carnival, which is often celebrated in February or March, gives people a chance to dress up as clowns, animals, and cartoon characters. During Carnival, Argentines build huge, colorful floats that parade down the street, with musicians, dancers, and onlookers enjoying the event. People also enjoy wheat, tango, and gaucho festivals. The Gaucho Festival of San Antonio de Areco is a popular event that takes place every November. Gauchos show their horseback-riding skills during a ten-day celebration that includes bronco riding, parades, and dancing. Another important celebration in Argentina is the national day of independence on July 9. Families and friends spend time together to honor the events of 1816. They celebrate with traditional food and parades. Gauchos: South American Cowboys Long ago, gauchos roamed the Pampas herding cattle. Today, gauchos symbolize the spirit of the Argentine people. Gauchos are proud of their horses. It has been said that “a gaucho without a horse is a man without feet.”
pages.brief: A Carnival parade moves down a street: performers dressed as clowns, animals and cartoon characters ride on huge colourful floats while musicians play and dancers follow, onlookers lining the pavements. Elsewhere gauchos in wide hats ride horses at a ten-day festival, a bronco bucking in a dusty arena, and families parade on independence day, July 9.

pages.text: As in other areas of Argentine culture, Spanish, French, and Italian immigrants to Argentina have brought their own tastes to what citizens eat. Today, foods from all these cultures are popular in Argentina. Since meat is widely plentiful, it is not unusual for people to eat beef twice a day. Steak and other cuts of meat are always available and are often grilled on an open pit or barbecue. Served nearly everywhere, empanadas are tasty pastries that can be filled with meat, vegetables, cheese, or fruit. Italian foods such as ravioli, pasta, and pizza are also popular. Besides food, another product consumed by Argentines is a tea called yerba maté. This drink is made from the dried leaves of the yerba maté plant. Argentines say it gives them energy and helps their minds stay alert. Food Argentine Tango The complicated movements of a dance called the tango tell the story of everything from love to political unrest. Every year in August, people come to Argentina from all over the world to take part in a tango festival.
pages.brief: Thick cuts of beef sizzle on a barbecue grill over an open pit, a plate of golden empanadas beside it, with bowls of pasta and a pizza on the table. A glass gourd of yerba maté tea passes between friends. In a hall across town a couple dance the tango in a close embrace while a crowd watches.

pages.text: Fountains decorate the area in front of the national government buildings of Argentina in Buenos Aires. Conclusion Solidly shaped by its European roots, Argentina has much to offer, including its beautiful land as well as its population, which has expanded to include people from China, South Korea, and other Asian nations. Argentines are committed to democracy and feel that their country will continue to prosper. A forward-thinking country, Argentina sets strict standards to protect the environment, encourages women to take part in government, and believes in equal rights for all people. Although political unrest has been a big part of the country’s past, its citizens—along with the rest of the world— hold great hope for its future.
pages.brief: Fountains spray and shimmer in front of Argentina's national government buildings in Buenos Aires, water arcing into a wide pool as people walk past across the plaza. Tall columned facades stand behind, and the city skyline of offices and apartments rises beyond the trees.

pages.text: Argentina Population: 43,646,358 Land: 2,736,690 sq km (1,056,642 sq. mi.) Capital City: Buenos Aires Primary Language: Spanish Primary Religion: Roman Catholic Primary Exports: beef, wine, soybean meal, cars, corn Name of Currency: Argentine peso.
pages.brief: A gathering view of Argentina's best-known products and places: cattle grazing on green grassland, a vineyard heavy with grapes beside a corn field, a modern car plant, and the skyline and port of Buenos Aires stretching along the wide brown river under a bright sky.

books.title: Petra
books.art_why: Petra’s ancient Nabataean city and its long history are best shown through drawing.

pages.text: Petra Above: Visitors wind their way through the steep canyon walls of the Siq. Cover: Visitors gather outside the Treasury in the ancient city of Petra, Jordan. Written by Kira Freed.
pages.brief: In a steep, narrow canyon, visitors walk in a line between towering red rock walls. Beyond the canyon, a crowd gathers outside a huge carved stone building with columns, the Treasury, in the ancient city of Petra, Jordan.

pages.text: Hundreds of artifacts are on display in Petra Museum, but many others have been lost to thieves over the centuries. It’s possible to see Petra in two days, but locals say five days are ideal. They advise tourists to be prepared to walk a lot, wear sturdy shoes, and bring sunblock, sunglasses, a hat, and a camera. Water is another necessity, as the desert can get extremely hot in summer. Petra is vulnerable to wind and water erosion as well as weathering caused by salt carried by wind from the Red Sea. The salt can enter small pores in the stone and then crystallize, causing damage. Tourists wear down surfaces by touching, sitting, and walking on structures. In 1985, the Rose City was awarded the status of a UNESCO World Heritage Site, which ensures its protection and conservation.
pages.brief: Inside the Petra Museum, rows of ancient artifacts sit on display. Outside, tourists in hats, sunglasses, and sturdy shoes carry water and cameras through hot desert stone paths, while wind and salt slowly weather the carved red rock surfaces.

pages.text: British author T. E. Lawrence wrote about Petra, “Till you have seen it you have not had the glimmering of an idea how beautiful a place can be.” Hidden City In the early 1800s, Swiss explorer Johann Ludwig Burckhardt became fascinated after hearing about a hidden city in the Middle East. Carved out of red sandstone cliffs streaked with gray and black, the city was in a narrow mountain valley in a remote part of Jordan and was familiar only to the Bedouin, Arab nomads who lived in the area. Disguised as an Arab for his own safety, since the area had periodic conflicts with neighbors, Burckhardt arranged to be taken to the mysterious city. He was rewarded for his challenging journey in 1812 after navigating a narrow canyon and entering the secluded valley. Burckhardt became the first European since the Crusades (1095–1291) to gaze upon the striking stone city of Petra.
pages.brief: A Swiss explorer disguised as an Arab rides with Bedouin guides through a narrow, shadowed canyon toward a hidden valley. Beyond, a city carved into red sandstone cliffs streaked with gray and black rises in a remote part of Jordan.

pages.text: Visiting Petra Petra is Jordan’s most popular tourist attraction. Over four hundred thousand visitors made the trip in 2015. The Rose City gained a great deal of publicity in 2007 when it was recognized as one of the New Seven Wonders of the World. Petra was also included on Smithsonian magazine’s 2008 list of “28 Places to See Before You Die.” Travelers buy tickets at the Visitor Centre and enter through the Siq by horse cart, on foot, or on a horse, donkey, or camel, as no motorized vehicles are allowed in the ancient city. People mainly explore Petra on their own, starting with the Treasury and moving on to tombs, the museum, and other sights. Petra’s Architecture Nabataean architecture is a synthesis of many different styles that reflect the region’s cultural influences, including those of Mesopotamia, Greece, Rome, India, and Egypt. The Treasury’s design elements reflect many different influences.
pages.brief: At the Visitor Centre, travelers buy tickets and enter the Siq on foot, by horse cart, horse, donkey, or camel, since no motorized vehicles are allowed. They move toward the Treasury, whose carved design blends influences from Mesopotamia, Greece, Rome, India, and Egypt.

pages.text: Little Petra Little Petra is a smaller archaeological site located 8 kilometers (5 mi.) north of Petra. Like Petra, it can only be entered by traveling through a narrow canyon and was created by Nabataeans who carved the buildings directly into the sandstone rocks. Many historians believe ancient traders stayed in Little Petra when they visited its larger and more famous neighbor to the south. A second theory is that carvers placed strong rods into the rock and used them to support a wooden board that they stood on while working. After completing a level, they would have placed the rods lower in the rock face and then moved the board. Scientists continue to look for clues in hopes of learning more about construction methods at Petra. Tools used by the Nabataeans included picks, chisels, mallets, and hammers. The use of claw chisels, which have teeth, could explain the coarse diagonal lines that are visible in many places in Petra’s stonework. Many stairways, water channels, and other features were also hand-carved into the natural shapes of the area’s cliffs and canyons.
pages.brief: In a smaller sandstone site north of Petra, narrow canyon walls lead to buildings carved into rock. Workers with picks, chisels, mallets, and hammers shape a cliff face, using rods and a wooden board to stand on while carving a higher level.

pages.text: Desert Treasure Petra is in southwestern Jordan, in a valley between the Dead Sea and the Gulf of Aqaba, a northern extension of the Red Sea. The ancient city is about 185 kilometers (115 mi.) southwest of Amman, Jordan’s capital, on what used to be important trade routes between the Middle East, Asia, and Africa. Petra is located in one of Earth’s driest deserts and is surrounded by dramatic red sandstone cliffs and gorges. The Siq (SEEK), a canyon 1.2 kilometers (0.75 mi.) long and up to 80 meters (262 ft.) high, leads to Petra from the east and is the city’s main access. The nearest year-round water supply is Ain Musa (“Moses’s Spring”), about 8 kilometers (5 mi.) away. A dry riverbed nearby is subject to occasional flash flooding. Petra EUROPE ASIA Petra AFRICA.
pages.brief: A wide desert landscape shows red sandstone cliffs and deep gorges in southwestern Jordan, with a long narrow canyon leading toward the hidden city. In the distance lie the Dead Sea, the Gulf of Aqaba, and a dry riverbed under a hot sky.

pages.text: The city of Petra gets its name from the Greek word for “rock.” Its nickname—the Rose City—comes from the color of the rock. The Rose City Petra spans 264 square kilometers (102 sq. mi.). The city center along the Colonnaded Street measures approximately 6 square kilometers (2.3 sq. mi.). Although the stone city is mainly carved out of sandstone cliffs, some construction was also involved. Among Petra’s features are hundreds of tombs, many adorned with sacred writings, as well as civic buildings associated with the city’s former function as an influential trade center. Many of Petra’s structures, which also include temples, monuments, altars, and houses, are over 30 meters (100 ft.) tall.
pages.brief: Rose-colored sandstone cliffs hold hundreds of tombs, temples, monuments, altars, and houses, many more than thirty meters tall. A central street runs through the city center, while some buildings are carved into the rock and others are constructed from stone blocks.

pages.text: The unfinished monuments have played an important role in helping scientists understand carving methods at Petra. One theory is that they removed large blocks of sandstone one level at a time, leaving a huge step and providing rock for constructing the freestanding structures. Carvers presumably would have used the rock step as a platform on which to stand as they worked on the highest level. Once that level was completed, removing another layer of raw material would have given carvers access to a lower level.
pages.brief: At an unfinished monument carved into a cliff, workers stand on a huge rock step left from removing sandstone block by block. They carve the highest level first, then remove another layer to reach a lower level.

pages.text: Building Petra Petra’s structures can be divided into two main types: freestanding structures and rock-cut monuments. Each type had its own set of construction challenges, but the rock-cut monuments, which were carved into Petra’s cliffs, no doubt presented the greater challenge and yielded by far the more impressive results. These architectural masterpieces were remarkable not only for their sheer size—the towering Monastery is 45 meters (148 ft.) tall—but also for their striking beauty and elaborate designs. Freestanding structures were constructed from the bottom up, while the opposite was true of rock-cut monuments. The top-down approach to carving monuments is confirmed by the city’s unfinished monuments, which are carved only on top. Because of Petra’s topography and geology, sandstone was the only abundant raw material for constructing buildings. No one is certain exactly how the Nabataeans carved the rock-cut monuments, although the shortage of trees in the area rules out the possibility of a plentiful supply of wood for scaffolding.
pages.brief: Carvers work high on a towering rock-cut monument, the Monastery, cut downward from the top of a sandstone cliff. Nearby stand freestanding buildings built from the bottom up, with little wood available for scaffolding in the bare landscape.

pages.text: Another significant aspect of Petra’s infrastructure is an extensive system of water management. The city’s dams, channels, aqueducts, cisterns, reservoirs, and tunnels are all evidence of highly advanced technology for the time for collecting, storing, controlling, and distributing water. The water-management system, which included a dam at the beginning of the Siq to keep floodwaters from flowing through the canyon and reaching Petra, allowed Petra’s inhabitants to thrive in a barren area. The technology is particularly impressive because the city supported at least twenty thousand people at its peak. In 1993, Petra was designated an archaeological park managed by Jordan’s Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities. The park includes ancient trade roads surrounding the city. Rock-cut channels along both sides of the Siq held pipes that carried water to Petra’s inhabitants.
pages.brief: Along the Siq, rock-cut channels carry pipes that bring water toward Petra. Inside the city, dams, aqueducts, cisterns, reservoirs, and tunnels collect and store water, allowing twenty thousand people to thrive in a barren desert landscape.

pages.text: The most notable structures in Petra’s city center include the following: • The Treasury ( al-Khazneh in Arabic) is Petra’s most famous monument and the first one visitors see when they emerge from the Siq. • The Street of Facades, which leads into the city center, is lined by tall tombs with large facades as well as some smaller tombs. Street of Facades Theatre • The Theatre, which was cut from solid rock, has sustained extensive damage. • The Royal Tombs, some of which are very ornate, are where kings were buried. • The Colonnaded Street runs through the center of the city. • Petra Museum, founded in 1994, contains more than six hundred artifacts that trace Petra’s history from various eras. • The Monastery ( al-Deir ) is among Petra’s largest monuments.
pages.brief: A wide view of Petra’s city center shows the Treasury, the Street of Facades lined with tall tomb fronts, a rock-cut Theatre, ornate Royal Tombs, the Colonnaded Street, the Petra Museum, and the huge Monastery among rose-red cliffs.

pages.text: The mosaics on the floor of the church depict many kinds of animals as well as figures representing the seasons, ocean, Earth, and wisdom. In 330 ce, Roman emperor Constantine I, a Christian, moved the Roman Empire’s capital from Rome to Byzantium (later Constantinople, now Istanbul) with the goal of spreading Christianity. Petra’s inhabitants slowly adopted Christianity, and the change was reflected in their city. Petra Church was built around 450 and remodeled in 500–550, and large mosaics were installed. During that time, some tombs were converted to churches. An enormous earthquake in 363 ce damaged much of Petra’s water-management system as well as nearly half the city. The earthquake was likely a significant cause of Petra’s decline. Another large earthquake occurred in 551. Arabs took over the region in the early 600s. By the end of that century, Petra’s last residents had left the city.
pages.brief: Inside Petra Church, a floor mosaic shows animals and figures representing the seasons, ocean, Earth, and wisdom. Outside, damaged stonework recalls the earthquakes that harmed the city’s water system and buildings before its last residents left.

pages.text: While Petra was thriving, the Roman Empire was expanding eastward into the Middle East. In 106 ce, the Romans peacefully took control of Petra. Evidence suggests that life in Petra continued much as it had previously. However, Roman rule influenced the city in numerous ways, including architectural design and new roads lined with columns. The Romans ruled Petra for three hundred years before moving the focus of their trading north and converting much of it to water routes. Those changes caused Petra to become less important as a trade center. The Colonnaded Street The Colonnaded Street, whose columns exhibit Roman influence, has sustained extensive flood damage over the centuries.
pages.brief: Roman builders raise columns along a new road in Petra after Roman rule begins in 106 ce. After three hundred years, the empire shifts its trade north, and the Colonnaded Street shows damage from centuries of floods.

pages.text: A Journey Through Petra Entrance to the Siq Visitor Centre Path through the Siq Treasury Street of Facades Theatre Royal Tombs Colonnaded Street Monastery Petra Museum Walking east to west from the Visitor Centre to the Monastery takes about twenty minutes at a normal pace. Most visitors take much longer, though, as they stop to examine each new location.
pages.brief: Visitors walk east to west from the Visitor Centre, through the Siq, past the Treasury, Street of Facades, Theatre, Royal Tombs, Colonnaded Street, and Museum, toward the Monastery. Many stop along the route to examine each new location, so the walk takes much longer than twenty minutes.

pages.text: A Bustling Trade Center The Petra area has been occupied since at least 7000 bce. The rock city was founded by the Nabataeans (nab-uh-TEE-uns), a nomadic Arabian tribe of camel, goat, and sheep herders whose stature in the ancient world grew during the first millennium bce. They slowly became successful traders who gained control of trade routes that linked various parts of the Middle East with Asia and Africa. Trading included incense from Arabia, spices from India, and silks from China. The Nabataeans provided water and shelter to traders transporting goods across the desert and charged tolls to foreigners. The Nabataeans were tent-dwelling nomads for hundreds of years before they began carving dwellings out of stone.
pages.brief: Nabataean nomads herd camels, goats, and sheep near tents in the desert. As traders carrying incense, spices, and silk cross the region, the Nabataeans provide water and shelter and collect tolls before they begin carving a stone city.

pages.text: At sunset on the winter solstice, sunlight illuminates the Monastery’s central podium. Over time, the Nabataean traders grew wealthy, built Petra, and settled down, although no one knows why they abandoned their nomadic lifestyle and became sedentary. Petra, their capital city, which they called Raqmu, is thought to have been founded around 300 bce and flourished starting in the first century bce. In addition to becoming a hub for people, goods, and money, the city also became a cultural center. At its peak, the Nabataean empire grew to include parts of modern-day Jordan, Syria, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and Israel. Not much is known about the Nabataeans apart from the fact that they worshipped the Sun. On the winter solstice and at certain other times of the year, the Sun illuminates or aligns with 80 percent of Petra’s main structures.
pages.brief: At sunset on the winter solstice, sunlight strikes the central podium of the towering Monastery. Below, wealthy Nabataean traders settle in their carved capital, Raqmu, while the Sun aligns with most of the city’s main structures.

books.title: Endurance on the Ice
books.art_why: Historical 1915 Antarctic expedition; drawn scenes suit the period survival narrative.

pages.text: Endurance on the Ice.
pages.brief: A sturdy wooden sailing ship, Endurance, sits among broken pack ice under a pale Antarctic sky. Ice presses close around the hull while the ship remains upright and still. No crew members are visible; the frozen sea stretches beyond the vessel.

pages.text: ICE ENDURANCE on t he.
pages.brief: The Endurance appears small in a vast field of cracked pack ice, its masts dark against the pale sky. Broken ice floes surround the wooden hull, and the horizon is empty. The scene suggests isolation in the Antarctic.

pages.text: Endurance became lodged in ice before the crew could reach the Antarctic mainland. Stranded Endurance was trapped. In January 1915, the ship had sailed into the Antarctic Circle and become stuck in the pack ice. The crew was certain that the ice would eventually break up and allow them to sail on, as it had done for other ships in the past. They trusted that their leader, the veteran Antarctic explorer Sir Ernest Shackleton, would guide them to safety. However, the ice continued to close in, and the sturdy wooden ship remained caught. Weeks passed, then months. Shackleton and the crew waited for the ice to liberate them. It never did. Now Shackleton and his crew faced a daunting task. They were trapped in the most isolated part of the world. No one back home knew what had happened or where to find them. In a time before satellite communications or long-range radios, there was no way to call for help. If they were going to survive, they were going to have to save themselves.
pages.brief: The wooden Endurance lies locked in thick pack ice inside the Antarctic Circle. The crew stands on the ice nearby, looking toward the trapped ship and the unbroken white expanse. No other ships or land are visible, and the scene feels isolated and uncertain.

pages.text: Lost in the Antarctic The Imperial Trans-Antarctic Expedition was the brainchild of Sir Ernest Shackleton. The plan was to land Shackleton and his team on the Antarctic coast, where they would travel by dogsled and attempt the first crossing of the continent. The mission belonged to a British tradition of exploration that had helped map and document much of the globe. Antarctica remained one of the least-known regions in the world, its harsh conditions requiring extensive supplies, careful planning, and great courage. Shackleton had the courage and was no stranger to the Antarctic. He had made a name for himself during two earlier expeditions there. He was a tough but fair leader who never asked anyone to do what he would not do himself, and his men respected him for it. The Heroic Age of Polar Exploration By the late eighteen hundreds, Western explorers had set foot on nearly every patch of land on the globe. The polar regions, though, still held many mysteries that attracted intrepid adventurers. Teams that included Ernest Shackleton had twice attempted to reach the South Pole, once in 1902, then in 1909. Each time, they were forced back. Finally, in 1911, Norwegian explorer Roald Amundsen and his team became the first to stand on the globe’s southernmost point. Only weeks after Amundsen’s achievement, British Robert Falcon Scott also reached the South Pole. However, Scott and his four companions died of starvation and cold on the return journey.
pages.brief: Shackleton and his team stand on the Antarctic coast beside dogsleds and supplies, ready to attempt the first crossing of the continent. Snow and ice stretch toward distant mountains. The men wear heavy polar clothing; the wide frozen landscape around them is severe and unknown.

pages.text: Shackleton had personally chosen Endurance, because he was impressed by the ship’s stout hull, which was designed to withstand and navigate heavy ice. He had also assembled a hardy and experienced crew. Captain Frank Worsley would prove an expert navigator in the most trying of circumstances. Frank Wild, Shackleton’s good friend, served as second-in-command. Other members of the team were likewise skilled and resourceful—essential qualities in a place as unpredictable as Antarctica. In August 1914, Endurance sailed from Great Britain. Four months later, on December 5, 1914, the ship left its last port on South Georgia Island in the far southern waters of the Atlantic Ocean. Just two days after leaving, Endurance encountered pack ice, which surrounded much of the continent. The ship plowed forward, using its engines and strong prow to bust through.
pages.brief: The Endurance sails from South Georgia Island into the far southern Atlantic, its stout wooden hull pushing through scattered pack ice. Captain Frank Worsley and Frank Wild stand among the experienced crew on deck, watching the frozen sea ahead.

pages.text: But on January 18, 1915, ice completely enclosed the ship. It was about 160 kilometers (100 mi.) from the intended drop-off point, but its destination might as well have been on the Moon. The expedition team could not possibly reach the continent from the spot where they were stuck. In addition, unusual storm patterns caused the ice to remain locked around the ship even when it should have been breaking up. Miles and miles of excess ice accumulated between the crew and any possible escape. By February, the men knew there was nothing to do but wait for conditions to change. On board Endurance, the twenty-eight men remained comfortable and in good spirits. It was a strong ship with a thick hull. They worked, read, listened to records on a phonograph, and organized talent shows inside the ship’s warm belly. They had plenty of food and other supplies to last for many months. The crew set their hopes on November, when the ice usually broke up. The crew play soccer on the ice to pass the time while the trapped Endurance looms in the distance.
pages.brief: Twenty-eight men play soccer on the ice beside the trapped Endurance, which looms in the distance. The ship sits locked in pack ice, while the crew passes time with games, reading, records, and shows inside the warm, well-stocked ship.

pages.text: Frank Wild surveys the wreckage of Endurance. Endurance did not last that long. In September, pressure ice closed in on the ship. Pressure ice consists of massive ice blocks driven by wind, currents, and storms. It started to squeeze Endurance like a nutcracker. The men on board despaired as the ship gradually tipped to one side. Its hull slowly bent, then cracked and split. The men compared the sounds it made to the moans and wails of a dying animal. In late October, the inevitable moment came. Shackleton gave the order to abandon ship. The crew salvaged a variety of useful supplies. Each man was allowed one set of clothing, plus his parka, two pairs of boots, and two pairs of mittens to protect against deadly subzero temperatures.
pages.brief: Frank Wild stands on the ice surveying the wreckage of the Endurance as pressure ice squeezes the ship. The wooden hull tilts and cracks, and the crew prepares to abandon it, gathering warm clothing, parkas, boots, and mittens against the subzero cold.

pages.text: The men also moved the three lifeboats from the ship to the relative safety of the ice. These boats were their only chance of ever getting home. To survive the trip, however, they would need more provisions. Shackleton felt tremendous responsibility to save his men. He planned to lead them across the ice on foot to an emergency cache of supplies for shipwrecked sailors. They set out on November 1 but didn’t get far. Steep ridges of ice two stories tall crisscrossed the landscape. The going was exhausting, dangerous, and finally impossible. Shackleton called off the march after only 3 kilometers (2 mi.). They set up camp on the biggest, most stable ice floe they could reach. In the distance, they could still see the skeleton of their wrecked ship. On November 21, they watched Endurance disappear beneath the ice. The men retrieved more supplies from their first camp; then Shackleton ordered another march in late December. Once again, they made little progress. They picked another large ice floe and pitched their tents, calling the site Patience Camp. They now knew they had no choice but to wait for the floating ice pack to convey them to a site where they could launch their boats. From there, they would try to sail to whatever land they could reach.
pages.brief: The crew hauls three lifeboats off the doomed Endurance onto a stable ice floe, then pitches tents at Patience Camp. In the distance, the wrecked ship's skeleton remains visible before it disappears beneath the ice. Steep ice ridges surround the camp.

pages.text: The men set up camp on an ice floe after moving supplies off the doomed ship. Patience on Ice Life at Patience Camp was harsh and unforgiving. Besides the extreme cold and frequent storms, the men had to contend with soggy gear and clothing. Most of the men slept crammed into five tents. Baths and clean clothes were out of the question. Despite these conditions, the men knew how to bear hardship. They entertained themselves by playing cards and sharing the few books they had. One sailor who had crafted a simple banjo led the rest in song. Food was always a favorite topic of discussion. Even though they were far from civilization, the men rarely went hungry. They ate two meals a day, almost always a calorie-packed stew called “hoosh.” It was made of crushed biscuits, water, a mixture of dried meat and fat called pemmican, and occasionally fresh seal meat and blubber.
pages.brief: At Patience Camp, men crowd into five tents on the ice floe, wearing damp, cold clothing. One sailor plays a simple banjo while others play cards and share books. A pot of thick hoosh stew sits nearby, made from biscuits, water, pemmican, seal meat, and blubber.
