pages.text: Hunting teams had good luck supplementing food stores with sea lions and penguins. Blubber—fat from the seals—also served as good cooking fuel. Meanwhile, the ice under them was moving with the ocean currents. Captain Worsley took regular sightings using his sextant, a navigational tool that measured the position of stars or the Sun to calculate location. Patience Camp was slowly drifting toward the edge of the pack ice, where they hoped to launch the boats. In March 1916, the men began sensing the rise and fall of the ice beneath their feet. By Worsley’s calculations, they had traveled more than 3,200 kilometers (2,000 mi.) since Endurance had become trapped. They noticed the ice becoming more fragile and prepared the boats in case they had to launch at a moment’s notice. Finally, on April 9, the long-awaited moment came, and they launched the boats into an opening in the ice. With some crewmates working the oars and others at the bow shoving aside blocks of ice, they drove for open water. Once they were in more open seas, they turned their boats toward Elephant Island. It was uninhabited and far from help, but any solid land improved their chances of survival.
pages.brief: Hunting teams return with sea lions and penguins while Captain Worsley takes sightings with a sextant on the drifting ice. The men prepare the lifeboats as the floe grows fragile, then launch into an opening in the ice and row toward Elephant Island.

pages.text: To Elephant Island Against the nightmare of the stormy Antarctic seas, Shackleton and his men pitted their muscles, minds, and willpower. With boats that lacked engines, their only propulsion came from two sets of oars and small sails. During the long, dark nights, the three crews worked to stay in sight of each other amid the monstrous waves. What followed was a voyage of agony and tenacity. As storms battered the lifeboats with hurricane-force winds and slashing sleet and rain, waves of freezing water crashed over the sides. Frost and ice crystallized on everything and everyone. The crews suffered from seasickness and frostbite. When crew members finished their turns at the oars, they huddled together for warmth. Sleep was all but impossible.
pages.brief: Three small lifeboats pitch through monstrous Antarctic waves under dark, stormy skies. Men pull at the oars and tend small sails, their clothing crusted with frost and ice. Freezing water crashes over the sides as the exhausted crews struggle to stay together.

pages.text: Worsley’s navigational skills in these conditions proved miraculous. On the seventh day, the high peaks of Elephant Island loomed dead ahead. The exhausted crew—men who had barely slept for seven days—finally made camp on a stretch of narrow, rocky beach. On April 16, 1916, for the first time in 497 days, the crew of Endurance set foot on land. However, they were still far from anywhere they wanted to be. There was no reason any ship would sail near enough to discover them. Someone had to venture on for help. Little more than a week after reaching Elephant Island, Shackleton, Worsley, and four others set out again in the James Caird, one of the lifeboats. Shackleton left Frank Wild in charge of the twenty- two men who waited behind. All their hopes were pinned on Shackleton’s dash for help. No one dared think what they would do if he failed. Ernest Shackleton Frank Wild Frank Worsley.
pages.brief: The exhausted crew makes camp on a narrow, rocky beach on Elephant Island, with high peaks rising behind them. Shackleton, Worsley, and four others prepare to set out in the James Caird, while Frank Wild stays behind in charge of the twenty-two waiting men.

pages.text: Across the Deadliest Sea The James Caird was modified for the voyage. The men had raised the sides and stretched a canvas deck across the top for protection against the tumultuous water. They had loaded supplies and hundreds of pounds of rocks into the lifeboat’s bottom. The extra weight would help steady the boat in rough weather. Their destination was South Georgia Island, the same place they had sailed from nearly a year and a half earlier. To get there, they would have to cross 1,287 kilometers (800 mi.) of the most treacherous seas in the world. Shackleton, Worsley, and four other crew members launch the James Caird and set out for South Georgia Island.
pages.brief: The James Caird is modified with raised sides and a stretched canvas deck. Supplies and heavy rocks are loaded into the bottom for steadiness. Shackleton, Worsley, and four crew members launch the small lifeboat from Elephant Island, setting out across treacherous seas toward South Georgia Island.

pages.text: The 6.7-meter (22 ft.) craft and its six-person crew had to battle for every mile. The waves were massive, and the weather battered them from every direction. The man working the rudder—usually Shackleton or Worsley—was often the only person with his head above deck so he could see. The others huddled down below, drenched from the steady wash of waves. Teams took turns managing the sails or working a hand pump to keep water from flooding the boat. Whoever was off duty attempted to steal moments of sleep near the prow. Several times, sleet and freezing rain layered the boat with ice, adding dangerous weight. Men risked their lives to crawl out onto the deck and chip it loose. Day after day, night after night, the boat plowed on. One night, Shackleton was at the rudder. Glancing back, he saw a line of white in the darkness above him. At first, he thought it was a break in the clouds. Then he watched in terror as the line rose higher. It was the crest of a gigantic rogue wave. He cried out, warning the men to hold on. It came down on them like a giant’s fist, flinging the boat forward. In an instant, the boat was half-filled with water. The men bailed with anything they could get their hands on. Ultimately, their desperate efforts saved their lives.
pages.brief: The six-man crew battles massive waves in the tiny James Caird. One man steers at the rudder while others huddle below, work the sails, or pump water. A huge rogue wave crashes over the boat, half filling it, and the men bail desperately to keep afloat.

pages.text: After seventeen brutal days at sea, they finally caught a glimpse of South Georgia Island—a most welcome sight. Again, Worsley had worked navigational magic in seeking out a small bit of land in the middle of boundless ocean. Beyond exhausted, the six men stumbled ashore. Unfortunately, they had landed on the western coast, but the whaling station was on the island’s other side. Sailing around the island was ruled too dangerous. Someone would have to hike 35 kilometers (22 mi.) for help, a feat easier said than done. Steep mountain peaks iced with glaciers divided South Georgia Island. No one had ever climbed them before. After some days of rest, three men set out— Shackleton, Worsley, and Tom Crean. They headed up the slopes and into the glaciers. Rock walls blocked their way and forced them to double back. The ice fields were so steep, they had to chop steps into the ice. Slowly, they slogged their way up until they reached the ridge of peaks that divided the island. They had just clambered over the ridge when Shackleton realized a different danger was closing in on them. They were on a high slope, night was falling, and the temperature was rapidly dropping.
pages.brief: After seventeen days at sea, Shackleton, Worsley, and Tom Crean stand on South Georgia Island's western coast. Steep, glacier-covered peaks divide them from the whaling station. The three men climb toward the ridge, chopping steps into the ice as night falls and the temperature drops.

pages.text: They needed to get to a lower elevation or they would freeze to death—and they needed to do it fast. With little debate, the three men sat down on the snowy slope and linked arms and legs. They pushed off and sped down the mountain on their backs. In less than two minutes, they dropped more than 305 meters (1,000 ft.). As they slid to a halt, the men burst into laughter, then rose and continued their trek. The next afternoon, on May 20, 1916, a trio of filthy bearded men in torn and tattered clothing walked into the whaling station on South Georgia Island and were led to the station’s manager. They had been hiking for thirty-six hours straight.
pages.brief: Shackleton, Worsley, and Tom Crean slide down a snowy slope on their backs, arms and legs linked, then continue their trek. The next afternoon, three filthy, bearded men in torn clothing walk into the South Georgia whaling station and are led to the manager.

pages.text: The twenty-two crew members wave to their rescuers from Elephant Island. They were marooned there for over four months. All Safe The twenty-two men back on Elephant Island remained cautiously hopeful. The earliest they expected rescue was in late May 1916, if Shackleton had been successful. May came and went, then June and July. As the days of August ticked off, the men feared the worst. Still, each day they tramped up to an overlook and scanned the sea. Each day they slouched back down, disappointed. Then on August 30, sharp eyes spotted a pillar of smoke on the horizon. The men hurried to get a fire burning to signal their location. The Chilean ship Yelcho steamed into view. The men watched as a small boat was lowered over the side, and they soon recognized a familiar figure in the prow. It was Shackleton, calling out to ask how they were. Some of the men wept with relief. Shackleton had led three earlier attempts to reach his stranded men. Each time, the ships were forced back by dangerous ice or mechanical problems. Determined to rescue his crew, Shackleton pressed on. Now, finally, he had made it back to Elephant Island.
pages.brief: The twenty-two men on Elephant Island wave from shore as the Chilean ship Yelcho steams into view. A small boat is lowered, and Shackleton stands in the prow calling out to his crew. Some men weep with relief after more than four months marooned.

pages.text: Twenty-eight men had sailed for Antarctica more than two years before. Now all twenty-eight were going home. Against tremendous odds— a wrecked ship, months in subzero temperatures on treacherous ice, and the crossing of deadly seas in small lifeboats—every single man who set out on Endurance had survived. It remains one of the greatest survival stories ever lived or told. Endurance Expedition: From Stranded to Rescued Endurance Expedition: From Stranded to Rescued 1 January 18, 1915: Endurance becomes stuck 2 October and November 1915: Endurance is crushed; sinks 3 December 1915: Crew founds Patience Camp 4 April 9, 1916: Sets out for Elephant Island in lifeboats 5 April 16, 1916: Arrives at Elephant Island 6 April 24, 1916: Sets out for South Georgia Island in James Caird 7 May 10–20, 1916: Arrives at South Georgia Island; crosses island for help 8 August 30, 1916: Yelcho rescues stranded crew ANTARCTICA.
pages.brief: All twenty-eight men of the Endurance expedition gather together, alive and safe after their ordeal. Their faces show relief and exhaustion as they stand against a cold, pale Antarctic setting, with a sense of hard-won survival and homecoming.

books.title: American Farms: Past, Present, and Future
books.art_why: The book spans historical farm life and future changes, so a drawn treatment fits.

pages.text: A Nebraska homesteader family stands in their celery field in 1904. Picture a Farm In 1901, John and Magreta Hoefer started a family farm on 160 acres (0.65 sq km) near Elgin, Nebraska. Their five girls and two boys would wake early before school to do their chores: open the henhouse, milk the cows, slop the hogs, and feed the horses. After school—especially in spring, summer, and fall—everyone hitched up their suspenders to tend to the gardens and fields. Almost all the work was done by hand and muscle, with horses to haul the wagons. It was a big effort to grow and raise enough food for their sizable family, enough feed for their livestock, and some surplus to sell.
pages.brief: A Nebraska homesteader family stands in a celery field in 1904, with five girls and two boys, John and Magreta Hoefer, on their 160-acre farm near Elgin. The children open the henhouse, milk cows, slop hogs, and feed horses; horses haul wagons beside hand-worked gardens and fields.

pages.text: Today, John and Magreta would be astonished to see what their small farm grew into. Their children, grandchildren, and great- and great- great grandchildren expanded their holdings and now manage more than 1,000 acres (4 sq km) of land split between seven Hoefer-owned farms. Today’s Hoefers do not need the whole clan to work the soil and tend to fields and livestock. They have a fleet of modern machinery and equipment, including big tractors, combines, and automated irrigation systems. Computers help them monitor and manage operations. They raise cattle and grow corn and soybeans as cash crops, along with specialty crops like popcorn and organic vegetables. American agriculture—and the U.S. economy overall—has changed dramatically in the last two hundred years. These shifts fundamentally altered what people do for a living and how they feed their families. Where once most everyone lived on a farm, now only a small percentage of Americans work the land. Yet American farms feed the nation, ship tons of food overseas, and are an important part of a global system of agribusiness. American farmers have shown a remarkable ability to adapt to change. They will need similar resilience to manage changes on the horizon.
pages.brief: The Hoefer family’s modern farm spreads across seven farms and more than 1,000 acres, with big tractors, combines, and automated irrigation at work. Cattle graze near corn, soybean, popcorn, and organic vegetable fields while a computer monitors operations from the farm office.

pages.text: A farmer guides a plow in Montana around 1900. Past: The American Tradition of Farming The United States was once a nation of farmers. In 1790, 90 percent of American families lived and worked on small farms. Their goal was to grow and store enough food to get through the winter, which required careful planning. A bad growing year due to drought, flood, or a disease of crops or livestock was not just a disappointment; it could mean hunger and financial disaster. Draft animals such as horses, mules, and oxen provided the power in front of a wagon or ground- breaking plow. Working the land also required constant human labor. On smaller family farms, entire families, from grandparents to young children, tackled the dawn-to-dusk chores that kept home and farm functioning. Others lived on larger farms, called plantations, enslaving people to work their land and produce commercial crops such as cotton or tobacco. Even with hard work, success or failure was often in the hands of unpredictable elements like weather and farm product prices.
pages.brief: Around 1900 in Montana, a farmer guides a ground-breaking plow behind horses, mules, or oxen while grandparents and children tackle dawn-to-dusk chores on a small family farm. In the distance, a larger plantation uses enslaved workers to produce cotton or tobacco.

pages.text: By the early 1900s, Americans were in the middle of a big social shift. The Industrial Revolution, which had begun in the late 1700s, was accelerating, with more and more people leaving rural farms for city factories. Interestingly, a revolution in farming helped make this possible. By 1900, the system of slavery had been abolished and family farmers made up only 38 percent of the country’s labor force. Yet even as that percentage shrank, farmers were able to grow enough food to feed millions in cities as well as their own communities. Three developments ramped up farmers’ productivity and allowed them to meet the growing nation’s food needs. The first, mechanization, was the direct result of technological development. Powered farm machinery allowed one person to do the work of dozens. Second, improved farming practices made it possible to grow more crops on less land. Farmers utilized improved seeds, chemical fertilizers, weed killers, and irrigation technology. Third, modern transportation systems allowed farmers to distribute their products over great distances. No longer were they limited to selling crops locally or regionally. Instead, they could truck them to trains or ships to reach national and even international markets.
pages.brief: As the Industrial Revolution accelerates, a rural family leaves its farm for a city factory. On the farm, powered machinery lets one person do the work of dozens; improved seeds, fertilizers, weed killers, and irrigation raise crops; trucks, trains, and ships carry products to national and international markets.

pages.text: The development of American agriculture was also aided by the nation’s expansion. Starting in the 1860s, the United States colonized the Great Plains. This wide region of prairies and other grasslands stretches westward from the Mississippi River to the Rocky Mountains. The land was mostly treeless with rich soil, making it ideal for farmers and ranchers to cultivate and exploit. It was easier to work than the rocky and forested areas back east. The Great Plains are still referred to as the “breadbasket” of the United States, even the world. This region is capable of producing vast amounts of food. Present: Family Farms as Big Business The trend toward fewer farmers producing more food has continued. Today, farmers and farm laborers make up only about 2 percent of American workers. Yet American farms produce more agricultural products than ever before. Farm size helps tell the story of American agriculture today. According to the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA), midsize and large-scale farms make up only 9 percent of American farms. However, they account for a remarkable 65.2 percent—nearly two-thirds— of food production.
pages.brief: A wide, treeless Great Plains landscape stretches from the Mississippi River toward the Rocky Mountains, with rich prairie soil where farmers and ranchers cultivate vast fields. A small number of farm workers manage large operations that produce abundant food, while midsize and large-scale farms account for most production.

pages.text: Despite the considerable size of some of these American farms, almost all of them continue to be owned and operated by families. Less than 2 percent of farms in the United States are “nonfamily farms” owned by outside corporations. Farm Size vs. Farm Production U.S. Farm Size by Income* U.S. Food Production by Farm Size 2.9% 1.3% 6.1% 10.6% 24.2% 42.4% 22.8% 89.7% KEY: Small Midsize Large-scale Nonfamily Family *The USDA defines a farm’s size by its income. Small farms generate $350,000 or less each year; midsize farms earn $350,000 to $999,000 annually; and large-scale farms bring in at least $1 million each year.
pages.brief: A graphic comparison divides American farms by size and income—small, midsize, and large-scale—and by ownership, family versus nonfamily. Nearly all farms remain family-owned and operated, with less than 2 percent nonfamily corporate farms; the comparison links farm size to shares of food production.

pages.text: However, most family farms are incorporated, which can offer important business advantages. Owners may pay less in taxes, be better able to secure bank loans, and have more protections if they have financial problems or the owners retire or die. Frahm Farmland Inc. is a prime example of a large-scale farm. Lon Frahm is its chief executive officer (CEO)—the top boss. His family has farmed in Kansas for six generations. When he took over the family farm in 1986, it had 5,000 acres (20 sq km) of cropland. Today, his team of about ten employees farms almost 27,000 acres (109 sq km). They grow corn, soybeans, wheat, and sorghum, a protein-rich grain used to feed livestock. Like many American farms, Frahm Farmland has greatly expanded its production in order to be successful and profitable.
pages.brief: Lon Frahm, chief executive of Frahm Farmland Inc., stands on his large Kansas farm, which his family has worked for six generations. His small team farms almost 27,000 acres of corn, soybeans, wheat, and sorghum; the operation has grown greatly from 5,000 acres in 1986.

pages.text: Corn, Cornier, Very Corny! More Food in the Field Productivity is a driving principle of every for-profit business, including agriculture. Through the years, American farms have continued to become more productive. Since the 1960s, the total number of U.S. farms has stayed fairly steady at about 2.1 million. The amount of farmland has stayed about the same as well. Yet during that period, American farmers have more than doubled their output of agricultural products.
pages.brief: Rows of corn fill a field as a comparison suggests the same amount of farmland producing twice as much agricultural product since the 1960s. The total number of U.S. farms stays fairly steady at about 2.1 million, and farmland area stays about the same while output more than doubles.

pages.text: Big farms like Frahm Farmland are the main producers of American foodstuffs. With good management, these operations are often more productive and efficient than smaller ones. They can produce more agricultural products per acre than smaller farms while on average spending less on land, equipment, supplies, buildings, and other operational costs. To operate as efficiently as possible, bigger farms have been at the forefront of farming technology in order to save costs on human labor. Examples range from robotic cow-milking machines to drones that monitor livestock to driverless tractors that navigate by global positioning system (GPS) as they work in the fields. Sensors measure ground moisture and automatically start and stop irrigation systems. Specially developed seeds, fertilizers, pesticides, and herbicides are other technological ways to maximize crop production, or yields.
pages.brief: On a big farm, a robotic machine milks cows while a drone monitors livestock and a driverless tractor steers by GPS through the fields. Sensors measure ground moisture and start or stop irrigation; specially developed seeds, fertilizers, pesticides, and herbicides help maximize crop yields.

pages.text: Keeping production costs low and profits high also helps explain why many large American farms employ immigrants as farm workers. Whether undocumented or legal guest workers, they are often paid wages far below those of American workers. To optimize efficiency, many big farms also practice monoculture—the intensive growing of one farm product, be it a crop or a breed of livestock. This approach allows such farms to invest only in the equipment and facilities that serve their purposes. Owners also develop expertise in the production of that product.
pages.brief: Immigrant farm workers, some undocumented and some legal guest workers, harvest a single crop on a large American farm for low wages. The operation practices monoculture, concentrating on one crop or breed of livestock, and invests only in the equipment and facilities that serve that single product.

pages.text: The risks of this scheme include catastrophic weather events and disease outbreaks that can wipe out that single crop. The lack of diversity degrades the soil and requires heavy use of fertilizers. It also leaves farmers vulnerable to significant drops in the market price of whatever they grow or raise. The Question of Factory Farms Some big livestock farms are designed to produce as many animals for slaughter as fast as possible. They are sometimes called CAFOs, short for “concentrated animal feeding operations,” or “factory farms.” Animals at these facilities are often held in small indoor pens with no natural light and little room to move about. Dairy cattle, hogs, and chickens are the livestock most often managed this way. Criticism of CAFOs focuses on three main issues: (1) these operations produce tons of animal manure, which harms the environment; (2) the animals are often raised and slaughtered in cruel conditions; and (3) the crowded conditions can result in disease outbreaks in livestock. To counter this, animals are given high levels of antibiotics, but this can result in germs resistant to antibiotics. Since people take in those same antibiotics when they eat the livestock, it can ultimately put their health at risk.
pages.brief: Crowded indoor pens hold dairy cattle, hogs, and chickens with little room to move and no natural light at a concentrated animal feeding operation. Tons of manure accumulate, animals receive high levels of antibiotics, and the crowded, often cruel conditions can lead to disease outbreaks and antibiotic-resistant germs.

pages.text: To offset their risks, about a third of American farmers sign production contracts with giant agribusinesses. The farmers agree to raise produce or plant seeds supplied by these powerful corporations. In return, the companies agree to pay the farmers a set price for the products. However, these contracts give the companies a great deal of control over pricing. They can also require farmers to make expensive upgrades to their facilities at the farmers’ expense. Farmers may even be put out of business for speaking publicly about how the company treats them. Farmers must weigh the costs and benefits of such production contracts. On one hand, these agreements offer some guaranteed financial backing for farmers’ hard work and investments. On the other, farmers can be left at the mercy of giant agribusiness. Even large-scale farms have limited power to negotiate terms with these corporations, which increasingly control not only agriculture but the food industry as a whole. How does the efficiency of big farms and food production affect the average American? In general, it means lower prices. The less it costs to produce milk, grow corn and wheat, or raise chickens and pigs, the more those savings can be passed on to consumers.
pages.brief: A farmer reviews a production contract with a giant agribusiness, which supplies seeds or produce and sets a price. The company controls pricing and can require costly facility upgrades; the farmer weighs guaranteed financial backing against being left at the mercy of the corporation.

pages.text: How Much Do Americans Spend on Food? Percentage of income Year The cost of food has gone up a lot since 1930. Yet by 1997, the percentage of their income that Americans spent on food had dropped to less than half of what it was early in that century. Future: Global and Local Farming Farmers often try to see the future. They invest in crops or livestock for the promise of future financial returns. They calculate whether investing in more acreage or a high-tech tractor will benefit their productivity. They check the weather forecast as well as the clouds to see whether they should cut the hay now or wait for the thunderstorm to pass. Planning ahead is a fundamental part of a farmer’s life. So what does the future hold for American farms and farmers? That depends on where you look. Two significant trends are shaping the future of agriculture in the United States—one global, the other local.
pages.brief: A line graph tracks the share of Americans’ income spent on food falling since 1930 even as food costs rise. Beside it, a farmer studies clouds and a weather forecast, calculating whether to cut hay now or wait for a thunderstorm while planning future crops, livestock, acreage, and equipment investments.

pages.text: Agriculture is now a global business, and most economists agree that globalization is shaping farming practices—in the United States and elsewhere. Globalization refers to the trade and movement of products and money between international businesses and banks. In many ways, it is already affecting what people buy and eat as well as how they make a living. For example, soybeans harvested in Nebraska or Iowa may be shipped to China, bringing Chinese capital, or money, to the United States. Avocados picked in Mexico are trucked to food distributors in the United States in exchange for U.S. dollars. Globalization offers expanded economic opportunities for American growers to sell more of their products overseas. At the same time, it creates risks that events in other countries will affect American farms. If the United States and China get into a trade disagreement, for instance, China can limit imports of American soybeans and corn. As part of globalization, giant agribusinesses are also reaching across borders and oceans like never before. They are buying or renting the resources they want and need wherever those resources may be.
pages.brief: Soybeans from Nebraska or Iowa are loaded onto ships bound for China, while avocados from Mexico are trucked to U.S. food distributors. International trade and money move between businesses and banks; giant agribusinesses reach across borders, and a trade disagreement threatens to limit American soybean and corn imports to China.

pages.text: In 2013, the Chinese conglomerate Shuanghui International purchased Smithfield Foods Inc. for $4.7 billion. Based in Virginia, Smithfield is the biggest pork processor in the United States. After the sale, China controlled more than four hundred farms, thirty-three processing plants, and one out of every four hogs in the United States, according to the USDA. Such international business deals involving food processors and distributors are likely to grow more common as globalization extends its reach. Even as large-scale farms go global, some smaller American farms are going in a very different direction—more local. Small farms make up almost 90 percent of American farms. However, they produce only 24.2 percent of farm products. About half of small-farm owners report that their main income comes from off-farm jobs. Some small farms are actually considered “hobby farms” that owners run more for enjoyment than profit. Still, the “local food” movement is turning up in more communities in the United States. A growing number of these farmers are shifting.
pages.brief: A large Virginia pork processing operation, Smithfield Foods, appears under Chinese ownership after a $4.7 billion purchase, with hundreds of farms, thirty-three processing plants, and one out of four U.S. hogs controlled. Nearby, a small American farm sells food locally, reflecting the contrasting local food movement.

pages.text: Instead, they sell what they grow at nearby farmer’s markets and restaurants. Many also choose to farm using more traditional methods, limiting or eliminating the use of chemical fertilizers, pesticides, and herbicides. Whether large-scale or small, though, future farm owners in the United States will need to grapple with environmental challenges. Agricultural experts worry that current farming practices are unsustainable because they are depleting valuable resources. Research indicates that farms in some areas are pumping too much water from underground wells and draining their sources. Some large-scale animal operations are generating massive amounts of pollution that are poisoning waterways and harming air quality. Overuse of fertilizers, pesticides, and herbicides is damaging valuable soil.
pages.brief: Small farmers sell what they grow at nearby farmer’s markets and restaurants and use traditional methods with fewer chemical fertilizers, pesticides, and herbicides. Around them, irrigation wells pump too much water, large animal operations generate pollution, and overuse of farm chemicals damages valuable soil, raising concerns about unsustainable practices.

pages.text: Soil—A Precious Resource Most people take for granted the ground beneath their feet. Not farmers. For them, soil is the lifeblood of a healthy farm. Without healthy land, crop yields tend to fall, along with the nutritional value of agricultural products. Good soil is much more than dirt. It contains organic matter—mostly decomposing plants and microorganisms that generate valuable nutrients for new growth. Research indicates that trying to replace these nutrients with chemical fertilizers has limited effectiveness and causes long-term harm to the soil. A small but growing number of farmers are changing practices to protect and improve their soil. More and more are doing no-till farming, which does not plow up fields. Instead, it allows the plant matter from the previous crop to decay naturally. These farmers may also rotate nutrient-restoring crops and let cattle graze in harvested fields, both of which help make and keep soil healthy. Practices that may produce a large harvest in the short term may do lasting damage to the land itself. More farmers now recognize these threats to their long-term prospects and are introducing more sustainable practices. They know a farm’s future is only as good as its land.
pages.brief: A close-up of rich soil shows decomposing plants and microorganisms creating valuable nutrients for new growth. In a no-till field, previous crop matter decays naturally; nutrient-restoring crops rotate nearby, and cattle graze in harvested fields, helping make and keep the soil healthy and protect the farm’s lifeblood.

pages.text: Climate change causes flooding (left) and desertification (right). Both hurt farmers. A bigger environmental issue looms on the horizon as well: climate change. Average temperatures are rising around the globe, and weather patterns are changing. Areas that once could plan on regular rainfall are seeing less precipitation, while other regions are receiving much more. Worldwide, climate researchers are observing an acceleration of cropland loss and growing deserts, especially in arid regions. Climate change is a contributing culprit. In the United States, studies indicate that climate change could greatly reduce farm productivity. By the year 2050, yields of corn and soybeans could drop by up to 25 percent in the Midwest. Such a decrease could have a significant effect on food supplies in North America and around the world.
pages.brief: A split landscape shows climate change’s effects: flooding on one side and desertification on the other. Corn and soybean fields in the Midwest suffer as temperatures rise and rainfall patterns change; by 2050, yields could drop by up to 25 percent, threatening food supplies in North America and around the world.

pages.text: By its nature, agriculture cannot adapt quickly to big, rapid changes. Farming, like most businesses, benefits from predictable conditions that allow for careful planning. However, the future is likely to bring bigger, more extraordinary variations in both economics and climatic patterns than American farmers have had to deal with in a long time—or maybe ever. A Changing Way of Life The business of American agriculture has been expanding since the nation’s founding. Farms have grown in size and sophistication. Their productivity has supplied a growing nation and helped feed a world population that has doubled since 1970 to almost eight billion people. Meanwhile, American farmers go about their daily work—planting seeds, growing crops, raising livestock, and producing the food we eat. Longtime farmers consider farming as much a lifestyle as it is a way to make a living. They find satisfaction in caring for their land, crops, and animals. That ethic has changed little in the last one hundred years. However, a generational shift is underway in terms of who owns and operates American farms. The average American farmer is fifty-eight years.
pages.brief: A longtime farmer plants seeds, tends crops, and raises livestock on an expanding American farm that helps feed a world population nearing eight billion. The farmer finds satisfaction in caring for land and animals, but a generational shift is underway: the average American farmer is fifty-eight years old.

pages.text: American workers retire. Fewer young people are choosing to farm. Even those with farming in their blood are walking away from the hard work, long hours, and unpredictable outcomes and income. Farmers will still be farming decades from now, adapting to whatever changes come. What their farms will look like at the end of this century—and who will be driving the tractors, picking the corn, and milking the cows—is more difficult to say. A farmer teaches his grandchild to drive a tractor. But will his grandchild still drive a tractor when they grow up?
pages.brief: An older farmer teaches his grandchild to drive a tractor on the family farm. Around them, fields and livestock suggest the daily work that fewer young people are choosing; the farmer wonders whether the grandchild will still drive a tractor when grown, and who will farm decades from now.

books.title: Ivory or Elephants
books.art_why: The book includes historical ivory-trade scenes and a 1925 hunting image where photographs of the events are impossible.

pages.text: This hippo is carved from ivory. Dubious Treasures Near the end of your tour of several Asian countries, you still haven’t found the perfect souvenir to bring home. You find yourself wandering along busy rows of tents, carts, and tables at an outdoor market. A table at the far end of the market catches your eye as you try to escape the noise. The table is lined with sculptures, mostly of animals. You ask about a couple of small white ones labeled “ivory.” They’re expensive, but they’re beautiful and small enough to carry on your long flight home. The vendor talks about the artist who made the ivory sculptures. He stresses how well-made the pieces are and how they will last forever. The vendor leaves out a few key details, however. He doesn’t tell you what ivory is or how it was obtained. He doesn’t talk about the illegal wildlife trade, which is crucial to the availability of the sculptures, or the brutal slaying of elephants.
pages.brief: At a busy outdoor market, rows of tents, carts and tables surround a far table lined with small white animal sculptures. A carved ivory hippo stands among them. A vendor gestures toward the sculptures while a traveler looks at the small pieces, thinking about carrying one home.

pages.text: What Is Ivory? Ivory is a hard cream-colored substance that makes up the tusks of elephants. Less commonly, the term is also used for the tusks of walruses, hippos, narwhals (a type of whale), and wild boars. Tusks are very long teeth that extend outside the mouth when it is closed. In most tusked mammals, the tusks are the upper canine teeth, but in elephants they’re the front teeth, or incisors. Tusks are made of a hard, bony tissue known as dentine. Enamel, a harder material on the tips of elephant tusks, wears away over time. Tusks grow continuously throughout an elephant’s lifetime. African elephant skull with tusks.
pages.brief: A close view shows a hard cream-colored elephant tusk and the skull it grows from, with the long tooth extending outside the mouth. Nearby, a walrus, a hippo, a narwhal and a wild boar are shown with their tusks. The scene explains what ivory is.

pages.text: Modern elephants are either African or Asian; African elephants are the larger of the two. African elephants are further divided into forest and savanna species. Males and females of both species grow tusks. The tusks of savanna elephants, the larger species, can grow to over 2.1 meters (7 ft.) in length. Among Asian elephants, some males have prominent tusks, while other males, as well as most females, have thin, short tusks that often break off. Tusks are a structural adaptation that give elephants a survival advantage. Elephants use their tusks to collect and transport food, to dig for roots and minerals, for display, and as weapons. Some elephants use them to dig water holes during the dry season. Tusks also offer protection for an elephant’s trunk. Tusks are deeply embedded in an elephant’s upper jaw. The only way to obtain an elephant’s tusks is by killing the elephant. Elephants use their tusks for many tasks, including digging (left) and lifting (right).
pages.brief: A large African savanna elephant stands with long curved tusks, while an Asian elephant nearby has shorter, thinner tusks. One elephant uses its tusks to dig for roots in dry ground; another lifts food with them. The tusks are deeply set in the upper jaw.

pages.text: About Elephants Elephants are Earth’s largest land animals, measuring up to 3 meters (10 ft.) at the shoulder. Male African elephants weigh as much as 6 metric tons (13,200 lb.). Although elephants look vastly different from us with their lumbering bodies and huge ears and trunks, they are extremely intelligent. Their brains are as large in proportion to their body—and as complex—as our own. They are among Earth’s most intelligent animals. Elephant Ancestry Elephants are the only living members of a family of mammals that also includes mastodons and mammoths, which are both extinct. Their closest living relatives are hyraxes— small, furred herbivores that look somewhat similar to prairie dogs. Other close relatives include manatees and dugongs, which look as though they would be more closely related to dolphins. Nevertheless, elephants, hyraxes, manatees, and dugongs all share a common ancestor.
pages.brief: A massive African elephant stands in open land, its ears and trunk huge. A small furred hyrax stands nearby, while a manatee and a dugong swim in water. The scene groups the elephant with its closest living relatives and shows its great size.

pages.text: Elephants are skillful problem solvers and tool users, often working together to invent new ways to do things. They live as long as some humans do—into their seventies—and have strong social bonds. Elephants maintain multigenerational family groups of females for life, guided by a wise older female known as a matriarch. She is responsible for keeping her family together, making sure they’re safe, and leading them to food and water. In times of drought, matriarchs have been known to find water holes they haven’t visited in decades. Elephants have complex emotions and have been observed laughing and playing. They also show great compassion toward each other. When an elephant feels distress, others stand next to her, soothe her with their trunks, and make soft, comforting sounds. These behaviors are notably similar to what humans do when a friend is in distress, except that we use a hand instead of a trunk. Elephants also display grief when a family member dies.
pages.brief: An older female elephant, the matriarch, leads a multigenerational family group of females across dry land toward water. Nearby, one elephant stands close to a distressed family member, soothing her with its trunk and making soft sounds. The group shows strong social bonds and care.

pages.text: Two young African elephants mourn the death of an adult female. Beyond their exceptional intelligence, elephants are vital members of the animal kingdom in another way as well. Scientists consider them keystone species—species on which many other species depend. Elephants play an essential role in keeping their ecosystems in balance. They dig water holes that also provide water for other animals. They clear land of trees and bushes, which creates more habitat for grassland species. The trails they create help keep fire from spreading and also assist with water drainage. In addition, some seeds must pass through an elephant’s digestive system in order to begin to grow, and their dung enriches depleted soil enough for people to grow crops. In short, elephants are essential to the ecosystems in which they live.
pages.brief: Two young African elephants stand beside the body of an adult female, mourning her death. Around them, a water hole, cleared grassland and new trails show how elephants shape their ecosystem. Seeds and dung enrich the soil, helping other plants and animals.

pages.text: An elephant hunter poses with his trophies in Sudan around 1925. The Ivory Trade Ivory has been prized by people for thousands of years and has been carved into art objects as well as jewelry and many other items. Although Asian elephants have been killed for their tusks— as well as their meat and skin—the ivory trade has a much greater effect on African elephants for two reasons: their tusks are larger, and both males and females grow them, so the supply is greater. Tracing the impact of the ivory trade on elephant numbers over the past two hundred years is sobering. In 1800, an estimated twenty- six million elephants lived in Africa. In the early 1900s, killing African elephants on safari was popular among wealthy Westerners. There was also a high demand for items made from ivory, including piano keys, pool balls, combs, and brush handles. According to National Geographic.
pages.brief: An elephant hunter in Sudan around 1925 poses with his large tusks and trophies. The scene is set in the historical ivory trade, when ivory was carved into art, jewelry and many other items, and African elephants were killed in great numbers.

pages.text: 1913 the United States’ consumption of ivory had reached about 181 metric tons (200 tn.) each year, and the number of African elephants had dropped to about ten million. In the 1970s and 1980s, the demand for ivory increased sharply again. An estimated one hundred thousand African elephants were being poached, or killed illegally, each year. Elephants were in serious trouble, and something had to be done quickly to stop their decline. Word Wise Poaching generally refers to the illegal act of hunting, capturing, or killing wild animals in violation of any law meant to protect wildlife. It includes illegally trapping or shooting animals on both public and private lands. Poaching most often takes place for commercial profit or for sport. Rangers and game wardens enforce anti-poaching laws.
pages.brief: A group of African elephants walks across a savanna while a ranger patrols nearby with binoculars. In the distance, fewer elephants stand among scattered tusks, suggesting illegal poaching and the sharp decline in their numbers. The scene shows the pressure of the ivory trade.

pages.text: In 1989, CITES (SY-teez), an international agreement that governs trade in endangered plants and animals, banned the trade of ivory. The ban dramatically increased public awareness about the elephant crisis. Prices dropped steeply as the demand for ivory plummeted, and elephant numbers started to recover. The global ivory ban had the potential to lead to the long-term recovery of African elephants. However, the increase in elephant numbers over the next ten years prompted four African countries—Namibia, Botswana, Zimbabwe, and South Africa—to ask CITES to allow them to sell their stockpiles of ivory. They claimed that elephant populations in their countries were either stable or on the rise. Furthermore, they stated that.
pages.brief: Leaders from many nations meet around a large table beneath a global map, marking an international agreement to ban ivory trade. In the foreground, elephant tusks are set aside, no longer for sale. The scene shows public awareness rising and prices dropping as demand falls.

pages.text: CITES approved a sale in 1999 but only to countries with strict guidelines preventing illegal trade. Japan was the only country that qualified. Another sale took place in 2008, this time with both Japan and China buying ivory. The second sale had the unintended effect of increasing the demand for ivory. It also gave the impression that ivory trading could again be legal at some point in the future. As a result, illegally killing elephants for their tusks skyrocketed, and many countries started stockpiling ivory in hopes of making huge profits down the road. Some countries have burned their stockpiles of ivory. Doing so ensures that the ivory will never be traded illegally.
pages.brief: Representatives from four African countries stand near stockpiles of ivory tusks, asking to sell them. In another scene, officials in Japan and China examine ivory purchases. Nearby, a pile of tusks burns, showing one country destroying stockpiles so the ivory can never be traded illegally.

pages.text: The crisis has been escalating ever since and has reached a tipping point: more African elephants are now being killed by poachers than are being born each year. Unless that trend is quickly reversed, it spells doom for elephants, not in some vague, distant future, but rather within our lifetimes. According to WildlifeDirect, fewer than 400,000 African elephants were alive in 2018, and 35,000 were being killed each year to satisfy the demand for ivory in Asian countries. If that rate continues, the ongoing slaughter of African elephants will guarantee their extinction by 2030. African Elephant Population elephant numbers (millions) 1.3 million 600,000 352,000.
pages.brief: African elephants stand in a savanna, but many are falling behind as poachers kill more than are born. A small calf walks close to its mother while distant figures of poachers and fallen elephants show the crisis. The scene conveys a tipping point and the threat of extinction.

pages.text: A caretaker walks with an orphaned elephant calf in Kenya. In addition to the looming threat of extinction, other tragic situations are also linked to the ivory trade. One is the trauma experienced by surviving elephants that witness killings and lose family members. As a result of that trauma, some elephants become aggressive and antisocial. Young males seem to be especially affected by the loss of mothers and older males. Orphaned adolescents have been known to go on killing sprees that target other young elephants, other species such as rhinoceroses, or humans. In addition, young females that have witnessed killings sometimes grow up lacking mothering skills and reject their babies. Given elephants’ high intelligence and strong social bonds, scientists aren’t surprised by their response to trauma.
pages.brief: A caretaker walks beside an orphaned elephant calf in Kenya, guiding it along a dirt path. The calf stays close to the caretaker, showing the trauma of losing its family. In the background, other young elephants stand apart, some aggressive and antisocial after witnessing killings.

pages.text: Another concern is the grave danger faced by rangers who protect elephants. Long ago, the term poachers generally referred to poor villagers who illegally killed a few animals to feed their families, and rangers often arrested them without incident. Today’s poachers are completely different, using state-of-the-art weapons in carefully planned attacks. In April 2016, an attack by heavily armed elephant poachers in Garamba National Park in the Democratic Republic of the Congo killed three rangers and seriously injured the park’s manager. Similar attacks have taken place in other parts of Africa. More than 450 rangers were killed by wildlife poachers between 2009 and 2017. In July 2018, an international ranger organization reported that 107 rangers had been killed during the previous year. Another consequence of poaching is a significant increase in elephants born without tusks. During a civil war (1977–1992) in the African country of Mozambique, roughly 92 percent of the 2,500 or so elephants in Gorongosa National Park were slaughtered for both ivory (to buy weapons) and meat (to feed the fighters), and most of the 200 or so surviving elephants lacked tusks. Under normal conditions, only around.
pages.brief: Heavily armed poachers move through Garamba National Park in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, carrying state-of-the-art weapons. Rangers patrol the same land, facing grave danger. The scene reflects the April 2016 attack that killed three rangers and seriously injured the park manager.

pages.text: African elephants are born without tusks, but since the war, more than 50 percent have been born tuskless. The occurrence of tuskless elephants has also increased in other African countries where poaching is common. The field of genetics helps shed light on this shift. Tuskless elephants are more likely to survive in areas where ivory poaching is common. Therefore, they are more likely to pass the trait of tusklessness down to their offspring. Normally it would take many, many generations for such a shift to take place. However, the high rate of poaching is causing the shift to occur much faster than normal by giving tuskless elephants an enormous survival advantage. At the same time, the situation raises the question of how elephants survive without tusks. Elephant scientists are just beginning to explore that question.
pages.brief: A herd of African elephants moves across a grassy plain in Mozambique, and many of the females have no tusks. A mother elephant without tusks stands beside her calf, showing how tusklessness is passed down. The scene suggests the rapid genetic shift caused by heavy poaching during the civil war.

pages.text: Other Threats As formidable a threat as poaching is to elephants, they are also at risk for other reasons. • Habitat loss – Long ago, elephants roamed great distances in search of food and water, following ancient migration paths. As humans have encroached more and more on their territory by building homes, farms, roads, railroads, and pipelines, elephants have lost a great deal of their range, and what remains is increasingly fragmented. Habitat loss and fragmentation not only prevent access to resources but also separate groups of elephants. This can limit their choice of mates and reduce genetic diversity, which is important to their survival. • Conflict with humans – Encroaching human populations also result in more elephant-human conflicts. Wherever elephants are not in protected areas, they compete with humans for food, water, and space. In some areas, elephants enter villages looking for food and damage crops and property. Farmers and villagers often kill or injure elephants while trying to chase them away, and elephants sometimes kill or injure people as well. • Culling – Conflicts with humans can become enough of a problem that wildlife managers kill a large number of elephants in order to control their numbers. Like poaching, culling often causes trauma in the elephants left alive.
pages.brief: Elephants move along a fragmented landscape where new homes, farms, roads, railroads and pipelines cut across their old migration paths. At the edge of a village, elephants enter fields looking for food and damage crops while farmers try to chase them away. In another area, wildlife managers cull a large group.

pages.text: Saving Elephants The effort to save elephants from extinction requires global action involving governments, organizations, and individuals. A key component is making sure that laws and regulations, both national and international, ban commercial trade in ivory. At the present time, CITES prohibits all commercial international trade in the ivory of both African and Asian elephants. A number of countries with significant ivory markets, including the United States, United Kingdom, China, and Singapore, either already prohibit commercial ivory trade or will enact bans in the near future. A significant step took place in December 2017 when China, once the largest ivory market in the world, banned all domestic ivory sales and closed its ivory-carving factories and shops. Other Asian countries that still buy and sell ivory are being pressured to follow suit. In addition to enacting bans, countries must also effectively enforce them. Carvings such as these are no longer sold in China because of the 2017 ivory ban.
pages.brief: Government officials and conservation workers stand outside closed ivory-carving shops in China, where carved ivory is no longer sold. Leaders from the United States, United Kingdom, China and Singapore discuss bans on commercial ivory trade. The scene shows national and international laws working to protect elephants.

pages.text: Eliminating the demand for ivory is another crucial piece of the puzzle. As long as demand is high, illegal ivory trade will continue, even with laws in place. Conversely, greatly reduced demand will cause ivory trafficking —and therefore the slaughter of elephants—to no longer be profitable. Conservation groups work tirelessly to educate the public about the plight of elephants. This is especially true in Asia, where demand continues to be high. While working to reduce the demand for ivory, various conservation organizations have reported that many people don’t know that elephants must die for their tusks to be taken. Public awareness campaigns are correcting that misconception. People march in April 2019 to end poaching and the illegal wildlife trade in Kenya.
pages.brief: A crowd of people marches in Kenya in April 2019, walking together to end poaching and the illegal wildlife trade. Nearby, conservation workers speak to a group about the plight of elephants and correct the misconception that elephants do not have to die for their tusks. The scene shows public awareness campaigns reducing demand.

pages.text: Elephant Heroes Many dedicated people are part of the effort to save elephants. Among them is Bryan Christy, an investigative journalist. Christy had a realistic fake tusk made that contained a GPS tracker. He planted the tusk in a region of Africa known for ivory poaching and tracked its path. Christy discovered that ivory poaching was being carried out by African terrorists— groups that use or threaten violence to try to achieve their goals—with the support of high-ranking people in government and the military. Conservation biologist Dr. Sam Wasser of the University of Washington in Seattle studies elephant DNA in an effort to combat poaching. For more than two decades, he has been using DNA from elephant dung to create a map of elephant genetics. The map allows him to identify where poached ivory is coming from and has helped law enforcement officials concentrate on those locations. Much of the illegal ivory from Africa travels to Asia through Hong Kong. In 2013, three Hong Kong schoolgirls—Nellie Shute, Christina Seigrist, and Lucy Skrine—formed a group to educate people about the connection between ivory and elephant deaths. They collected more than eighteen thousand signatures on a petition to urge Hong Kong’s government to destroy its huge stockpile of ivory, which had been seized from smugglers. The task, which was completed in 2016, was one of the largest known ivory destruction projects in the world.
pages.brief: Investigative journalist Bryan Christy holds a realistic fake tusk fitted with a GPS tracker. In another scene, conservation biologist Dr. Sam Wasser studies elephant dung and a DNA map while three Hong Kong schoolgirls collect petition signatures. The scene shows heroes working to trace poached ivory and destroy stockpiles.

pages.text: Working with local communities is another part of the effort to save elephants. People who have had conflicts with elephants often have negative attitudes toward them. These people benefit from support to deal with the problems so that killing isn’t the only option. Conservation organizations educate local people about elephant habits and habitats, along with the danger of extinction from poaching and habitat loss. They provide information about how to live in harmony with elephants. For example, one organization teaches farmers to plant red pepper around their crops. This plant bothers the eyes and noses of elephants and causes them to leave the area. Conservation organizations also encourage people to consider elephants as a precious resource of their country—one they can take pride in that can also attract tourists and become a source of income. In addition, organizations connect with young people and inspire them to help elephants survive.
pages.brief: Conservation workers meet with local farmers beside a field, showing them how to plant red pepper around crops to keep elephants away. Nearby, villagers and elephants share the land without conflict, and young people learn to see elephants as a precious resource that can attract tourists and bring income.

pages.text: Three elephants in Botswana approach a water hole at sunset. Time Is Running Out Now imagine that outdoor Asian market again, with its beautiful ivory sculptures. People who don’t know where ivory comes from will keep buying it, and elephant numbers will continue to drop. The severe decline of elephant populations is a complex topic and also a controversial one. Disagreement exists about whether to ban all ivory trade or regulate it. Some people think the only way to save elephants is with a total ivory ban. Others believe that a total ban will increase the illegal ivory trade, drive ivory prices higher, and create more incentive for poachers to keep killing elephants. Will time run out for elephants while people struggle to find answers? The clock is ticking. For now, two things are certain: elephants are being slaughtered at a rate of about a hundred each day, and a world without elephants would be an impoverished place to live.
pages.brief: Three elephants in Botswana approach a water hole at sunset, their shadows long on the ground. In the mind's eye, the outdoor Asian market returns with beautiful ivory sculptures on a table while elephant numbers continue to drop. The scene asks whether time will run out for elephants.

books.title: Volcanoes
books.art_why: Historical eruption scenes and cutaway diagrams are best shown in drawings.

pages.text: This volcano shows signs of activity. The Eruption of Vesuvius Few people in the Roman city of Pompeii were alarmed by the earthquakes that began shaking the region in 79 ce. They had endured seismic activity in the past and had rebuilt their city whenever any significant damage occurred. Usually, though, the earthquakes were minor, and people had grown accustomed to them. The residents of Pompeii loved their beautiful city and would not leave just because the ground occasionally shook or a building fell down. No one connected the trembling ground with the plume of smoke that steadily hissed from nearby Mount Vesuvius. After all, people had lived in Pompeii for centuries without ever witnessing a volcanic eruption, and the slopes of Mount Vesuvius were teeming with life and were covered with trees, flowers, and grass. It had been a thousand years since the volcano had erupted, so most people assumed that it was dormant, or even extinct.
pages.brief: An active volcano with smoke rising from its summit looms over a Roman city. In Pompeii, people go about daily life among buildings while the ground trembles slightly. Nearby Mount Vesuvius has green slopes covered with trees, flowers, and grass. The city looks beautiful and calm beneath the smoky plume.

pages.text: But everything changed on August 24 around one o’clock in the afternoon. Suddenly, a tremendous explosion shook the area around the mountain, sending molten rock, ash, and dust spewing from the summit of the volcano and darkening the sky. This dust, ash, and stone (collectively known as tephra ) rained down on the city, covering the ground as far away as 16 kilometers (10 mi.) from the mountain. By three o’clock, lava gushed from the mouth of the volcano at an alarming rate, destroying everything in its path. By six o’clock, the cloud of dust and ash had ascended to 32 kilometers (20 mi.) in height, and the swirling energy inside it generated lightning bolts. The ash continued to blanket the area, covering the ground to a depth of 1 meter (3.3 ft.) and causing buildings to collapse under the weight of the falling debris. Mount Vesuvius overlooks the excavated ruins of Pompeii.
pages.brief: Mount Vesuvius explodes at one o’clock, hurling molten rock, ash, and dust into a dark sky. A towering ash cloud swirls with lightning above the mountain as lava gushes down its slopes. Ash rains over the region, collapsing buildings under its weight. Below, excavated ruins of Pompeii lie near the volcano.

pages.text: People in the cities surrounding Mount Vesuvius tried to evacuate the area as the volcano demolished their homes and farms. They gathered their valuables and most portable treasures and hurried their families away from the disaster. Some people tried to traverse the thick layers of ash that covered the ground, but the ash was so deep and so hot that many people died. Others were struck and killed by stones falling from the dark sky, and some suffocated on the ash- and dust-clogged air. Around midnight, the crisis grew even worse. The massive cloud of ash, poisonous gases, glowing-hot dust, and smoke had become so dense and heavy that it could no longer remain airborne. The cloud collapsed into a pyroclastic flow, racing down the mountain at speeds of up to 500 kilometers per hour (310 mph). Glowing-hot lava bubbles up inside a volcano.
pages.brief: Families flee cities around Mount Vesuvius, carrying valuables and portable treasures away from collapsing homes and farms. Some people struggle through deep, hot ash or fall beneath falling stones. Near midnight, a dense cloud of ash, poisonous gas, and glowing dust races down the mountain as a pyroclastic flow. Inside the volcano, glowing-hot lava bubbles.

pages.text: A plaster cast of the body of an inhabitant of Pompeii who perished during the eruption of Mount Vesuvius Do You Know? Pompeii, a city not far from Mount Vesuvius, was completely buried by a surge cloud. Many perished under the surge cloud, but as their bodies decayed, they left air pockets in the hardened ash and mud that surrounded them. These air pockets preserved the exact shapes of the bodies they once contained. Archaeologists filled the holes with plaster to make casts showing how the people looked when they died. This was Mount Vesuvius’s first surge cloud, which within a few moments scorched and buried the people in the cities of Pompeii and Herculaneum as it swept over them like a wave. As more dust and ash billowed from the volcano, more surge clouds followed. When the eruption was over, two cities of the Roman Empire were completely buried and wiped off the face of the Earth. They would not be rediscovered for over a thousand years.
pages.brief: A plaster cast shows the shape of a Pompeii inhabitant who died during the eruption. Archaeologists work with hardened ash and mud, filling empty spaces left by bodies with plaster. A scorching surge cloud sweeps over Pompeii and Herculaneum like a wave, burying the cities. More ash and surge clouds follow until both Roman cities disappear.

pages.text: What you just read is an account of a real event, but how did it happen, and what could cause such a catastrophic explosion? And if volcanoes are so dangerous, why do people choose to live near them? People and Volcanoes People live near volcanoes for a variety of reasons. They often find nutrient-rich soil for farming in these regions or wonderful hot springs where they can take relaxing baths. Still, people have learned over time to respect volcanoes. Long ago, people had no way to scientifically predict or understand volcanoes, but volcanoes were woven into their beliefs, traditions, and lore. For instance, in Indigenous Hawaiian culture, there are legends about the goddess Pele (PAY-lay), whose anger caused volcanoes to erupt. Some types of volcanic glass, such as Pele’s hair and Pele’s tears, are named in honor of this goddess. Pele’s tears are small drops of lava that cool and become solid while flying through the air.
pages.brief: People farm in nutrient-rich volcanic soil and relax in hot springs near volcanoes. In Indigenous Hawaiian culture, the goddess Pele is shown in a legend, her anger causing volcanoes to erupt. Small drops of lava cool into solid glass called Pele’s tears, while thin threads of volcanic glass are named Pele’s hair. People respect the volcano around them.

pages.text: Devil’s Tower is an extinct volcano in Wyoming that holds deep spiritual significance for many Indigenous tribes of the Great Plains. The Lakota call it Bear Lodge, while the Kiowa call it Tree Rock. It is considered a sacred place of creation and renewal where pilgrims make offerings, pray, and perform ceremonies. In ancient Rome, people believed that the Roman god Vulcan worked in a blacksmith’s forge beneath Earth’s surface. They saw volcanoes as the chimneys of the underground forge where Vulcan fashioned lightning bolts for use by Jupiter, the king of the gods, and made weapons and armor for Mars, the god of war. The word volcano comes from the name Vulcan. Even today, volcanologists say that volcanoes smell like a blacksmith’s forge. In Japanese Shinto and Buddhist traditions, Mount Fuji holds great spiritual significance. It is considered a stairway to another world and revered as the spiritual home of Kono-hana, a Shinto deity. It has become a sacred center for both pilgrimage and art in Japan. Devil’s Tower, also known as Bear’s Lodge and Tree Rock, is an extinct volcano in Wyoming.
pages.brief: Devil’s Tower in Wyoming is sacred to Indigenous tribes of the Great Plains, where pilgrims pray and make offerings. In Roman belief, the god Vulcan works a blacksmith’s forge beneath Earth, and volcanoes are its chimneys. Mount Fuji in Japan is a sacred Shinto and Buddhist site, a stairway to another world, and a center for pilgrimage and art.

pages.text: While volcanoes remain spiritually and symbolically significant in many cultures, today scientists are also able to use tools and instruments to learn more about how they develop and function. Scientists can even predict when volcanoes will next erupt. Where and Why Volcanoes Form The first volcanoes appeared about 3.5 billion years ago, covering vast areas with hot lava that spewed from deep within Earth. Earth’s hard surface, or crust, is made of many continent-sized sheets of rock called tectonic plates. Some plates make up the continents themselves, while others make up the ocean floors. Just under the surface of the plates, the Earth is extremely hot (about 1,200° Celsius or 2,192° Fahrenheit)—so hot that rock melts into a liquid called magma. Sometimes, the magma forces its way up to the surface and seeps out through cracks in the crust, causing volcanoes to form. vents magma chamber.
pages.brief: Scientists use instruments to study volcanoes and predict eruptions. Long ago, hot lava spewed from deep within Earth and covered vast areas. Earth’s crust is made of giant rock sheets called tectonic plates. Beneath them, intense heat melts rock into magma, which sometimes rises through cracks in the crust to form a volcano.

pages.text: Plate Movement Volcanic arc Trench Oceanic crust Mantle Mantle When an ocean plate crashes into a continental plate, the ocean plate moves down, creating an active volcanic region. Scientists estimate that more than fifteen hundred different volcanoes have erupted in the last ten thousand years, and every year about thirty-five or forty volcanoes erupt around the world. Sometimes the only sign of volcanic activity is a small amount of smoke or steam emerging from a volcano. Some volcanoes are always erupting slowly, while others, like Vesuvius, can remain quiet for hundreds or even thousands of years between explosive eruptions. Volcanoes usually form at the edges of tectonic plates, which are slowly floating on the thick, liquid magma underneath them. But the various plates are moving in different directions, and as they move, they can crash into, pull away from, or grind past other plates. As the huge plates slide and rub against each other, their movements create large cracks in the crust where magma can break through to form volcanoes.
pages.brief: An ocean plate crashes into a continental plate and moves downward, creating an active volcanic region. More than fifteen hundred volcanoes have erupted in the last ten thousand years, and about thirty-five or forty erupt each year. Volcanoes usually form at the edges of tectonic plates, where moving plates create cracks that let magma break through.

pages.text: Pacific Ocean EQUATOR More than half the active volcanoes in the world occur along the Ring of Fire. Ring of Fire There are at least five hundred active volcanoes in the world, most of which are located near the edges of tectonic plates. The edge of the Pacific Ocean plate is a particularly dense volcanic region known as the Ring of Fire. Another notably active volcanic region runs along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, which is a mountain chain in the Atlantic Ocean. Two plates are drifting apart in the Atlantic Ocean, allowing magma to seep up through the ocean floor, where it accumulates. Over time, the magma can build up and create mountains so tall that they emerge from the water. The country of Iceland sits atop the summits of large volcanoes in the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.
pages.brief: A map-like view of the Pacific Ocean shows the Ring of Fire, a dense volcanic region along the edge of the Pacific plate, where more than half the world’s active volcanoes occur. In the Atlantic Ocean, the Mid-Atlantic Ridge forms a mountain chain where two plates drift apart, magma seeps up, and volcanoes rise. Iceland sits atop large volcanoes there.

pages.text: Other volcanoes are located in areas far away from the edges of the plates. For example, the islands of Hawai‘i are in the center of the Pacific Ocean plate. They are located above a “hot spot,” a place where hot magma sits very close to the surface of Earth’s crust. Sometimes the magma creates a new island, but the process is gradual, taking tens or even hundreds of thousands of years. In Yellowstone National Park, in the middle of the North American plate, an underground hot spot sits directly beneath underground lakes and waterways. The magma heats up the ground and the water in this area like a giant teapot, creating geysers and hot springs. You can visit Yellowstone in Wyoming and see water erupting from the ground at geysers such as Old Faithful. Hawai‘i Kauai hot spot plate movement Kauai Hawai‘i.
pages.brief: The Hawaiian Islands rise in the middle of the Pacific plate above a hot spot, where magma sits close to the surface and can slowly build new islands. At Yellowstone National Park in Wyoming, a hot spot beneath underground water heats the ground like a giant teapot, creating geysers and hot springs such as Old Faithful.

pages.text: Different volcanoes erupt in different ways, depending on where and why the volcano forms. Some volcanoes erupt gently and gradually, while others suddenly explode with the force of many atomic bombs. Let’s examine different kinds of volcanoes and learn how they erupt. Composite Volcanoes Mount Vesuvius, which you read about earlier, is a composite volcano on the west coast of southern Italy. Composite volcanoes are explosive volcanoes—their eruptions can be extremely violent and destructive. Also called stratovolcanoes, they are the most common type of volcano. They are usually very large mountains with steep sides and evenly shaped peaks, often with a bowl- shaped crater at the top. The crater is a hollow area where the magma, hot gases, and ash come out. The impressive shape of a composite volcano.
pages.brief: Mount Vesuvius in southern Italy is a composite volcano with steep sides and an evenly shaped peak. A bowl-shaped crater sits at the top, where magma, hot gases, and ash come out. Composite volcanoes, also called stratovolcanoes, are the most common type and can erupt with extreme violence and destruction. One stands as an impressive mountain.

pages.text: Mount St. Helens before 1980 eruption Mount St. Helens after 1980 eruption Do You Know? When Mount St. Helens, in Washington State, erupted on May 18, 1980, sixty-three people died and 311 square kilometers (193 sq mi.) of forest were flattened by hot winds that blew down the mountainside. Most composite volcanoes occur where the magma near the surface is viscous —thick and slow moving like syrup. Magma moves toward the surface in tubes called vents. When the magma is unusually thick, it can cool and harden inside the vent, plugging the vent and trapping the magma below. Because the heat and gases beneath the plugged vent have nowhere to go, the pressure slowly begins to increase. Eventually the pressure becomes so great that it reaches a critical threshold, and the volcano explodes. Sometimes the explosion is so violent that the whole mountain is destroyed in the blast. When Washington State’s Mount St. Helens erupted in 1980, the entire northern side of the mountain was obliterated.
pages.brief: Mount St. Helens is shown before and after its 1980 eruption, when sixty-three people died and hot winds flattened 311 square kilometers of forest. Thick, slow-moving magma can harden inside a vent and trap pressure beneath it. When the pressure reaches a critical threshold, the volcano explodes. The blast obliterated the entire northern side of Mount St. Helens.

pages.text: When composite volcanoes erupt, they send massive clouds of ash, dust, smoke, hot gas, and rock into the air. These clouds rise for many kilometers, turning the sky black and raining ash onto the ground. When a cloud of debris becomes too dense to remain in the air, it collapses in a violent surge cloud. Many composite volcanoes are very tall, and they are often capped with ice and snow. In an instant, an explosion can melt all the ice and snow on the top of the volcano, sending a flood of water, mud, and rock racing down the mountain at up to 100 kilometers per hour (62 mph). Such a mudslide triggered by volcanic activity is known as a lahar. Melting ice and snow sent a massive lahar racing down the side of this volcano.
pages.brief: A composite volcano sends massive clouds of ash, dust, smoke, hot gas, and rock high into the air, turning the sky black and raining ash onto the ground. Ice and snow cap the tall mountain. An explosion melts them, sending a flood of water, mud, and rock racing down the slope as a lahar.

pages.text: Crater Lake is a well-known caldera in Oregon. This huge caldera was formed when the volcano collapsed in on itself. Do You Know? The Klamath people in southern Oregon have passed down a legend about the origin of Crater Lake. According to their tradition, the first coyote fell in love with a star and found a way to join her in the sky. When he fell back to Earth, his impact made a hole that became Crater Lake. Some volcanic ash clouds are so gigantic that the ash and dust can travel around the world, blocking out sunlight and cooling down the entire planet. After the 1815 eruption of Tambora, a volcano in Indonesia, people living as far away as North America experienced a cold, snowy summer. Sometimes an entire underground lake of magma can pour out of a composite volcano, leaving a huge empty space below. With nothing to support it, the surface collapses into the empty chamber, leaving a large bowl-shaped basin called a caldera. Calderas can measure as much as 100 kilometers (62 mi.) from side to side. Over time, they often fill with water, creating large lakes such as Crater Lake in Oregon.
pages.brief: Crater Lake in Oregon fills a huge caldera where a volcano collapsed inward. In a Klamath legend, the first coyote falls back to Earth and makes the hole that becomes the lake. Volcanic ash clouds can circle the world and cool the planet. A caldera forms when magma drains away and the surface collapses, later filling with water.

pages.text: Composite volcanoes can destroy huge forests, bury entire cities, and even result in human deaths. These volcanoes are very dangerous because they often remain quiet for hundreds of years between eruptions.
