People forget that the volcano might erupt, and they build their homes dangerously close to the mountain. Shield Volcanoes You may have seen a video of bright orange lava flowing or spraying from the top of a volcano. The lava, which is very runny, flows smoothly and quickly, moving like water in a stream. The lava spreads out over the land before slowly hardening and building up. This type of lava comes from a shield volcano. Shield volcanoes usually have gentle, smooth mountain slopes in the shape of shields. Mauna Loa, a shield volcano in Hawai‘i.
pages.brief: Composite volcanoes can destroy forests, bury cities, and kill people, yet they often stay quiet for hundreds of years while homes are built close by. A shield volcano sends runny orange lava flowing smoothly like a stream, spreading out before it hardens. Shield volcanoes have gentle, smooth slopes shaped like shields. Mauna Loa in Hawai‘i is one.

pages.text: Olympus Mons, on the surface of Mars, is the largest known volcano in the solar system. It would cover the entire state of Arizona. Eruptions of shield volcanoes are usually gentle rather than explosive, although the lava flows can still destroy roads, homes, and forests. Sometimes a shield volcano contains hot gases or steam that sprays from the crater, creating a bright lava fountain. Since the paths of the lava flows are stable and predictable, scientists are often able to get very close to study them. Shield volcanoes can remain quietly active for long periods of time and grow to become extremely large in the process. Mauna Loa on Hawai‘i is the tallest volcano in the world, rising 9,170 meters (30,080 ft.) from its base on the seafloor, making it taller than Mount Everest. If Mauna Loa erupts again, it could grow even taller. However, even Mauna Loa seems tiny when compared to the largest known volcano in our solar system—Olympus Mons on Mars. This enormous Martian shield volcano stands 27 kilometers (17 mi.) tall.
pages.brief: Olympus Mons on Mars is the largest known volcano in the solar system, large enough to cover Arizona and twenty-seven kilometers high. Shield volcanoes erupt gently, though lava flows can destroy roads, homes, and forests. Steam or hot gas can spray from a crater as a bright lava fountain. Mauna Loa in Hawai‘i is the tallest volcano on Earth.

pages.text: Cinder Cones and Lava Domes Some volcanoes are not active long enough to form large mountains. Instead, they may just spray small bits of lava into the air for brief periods of time. The small lava chunks and bits of ash harden into lightweight black rocks called cinders. The cinders pile up around the vent into a cone-shaped hill with a crater at the top. Such hills are called cinder cones. Brand-new volcanoes that suddenly appear often form cinder cones. Other cinder cones pile up inside the craters or calderas of larger, older volcanoes. Most cinder cones erupt only once. Because cinder cones are made of loose rocks, they usually erode quickly in the wind and rain. Cinder cones at Mauna Kea volcano, Hawai‘i.
pages.brief: Small bits of lava and ash spray into the air, harden into lightweight black cinders, and pile around a vent to form a cone-shaped hill with a crater at the top. These cinder cones can appear suddenly, sometimes inside craters or calderas of larger volcanoes. Most erupt only once, and loose rocks erode quickly. Cinder cones stand at Mauna Kea.

pages.text: Lava dome atop Novarupta vent, Katmai National Park and Preserve, Alaska (above); a scientist monitoring a lava dome inside a crater Lava domes also result from small, brief eruptions, but the lava that forms these structures is a thick, pasty liquid that oozes from the vent and quickly hardens. Sometimes, more lava pushes up and expands through the center of the dome, cracking the outside. These domes often form in areas with other volcanic activity. They are often found in the craters and calderas of larger volcanoes. Like composite volcanoes, lava domes often explode violently.
pages.brief: A lava dome sits atop the Novarupta vent in Alaska, while a scientist monitors a lava dome inside a crater. Lava domes form from small eruptions of thick, pasty lava that oozes out and hardens. More lava can push through the center and crack the outside. They often form in larger volcanoes and can explode violently.

pages.text: Conclusion Volcanoes are the most spectacular evidence we have that Earth is a changing planet. Lava pouring from a volcanic vent creates new rock and new land, and volcanic ash makes extremely fertile soil that is useful for farming. In some places, people use the geothermal energy from volcanoes to run power plants and produce electricity. Some people even live inside volcanoes. Rabaul, Papua New Guinea, is a port city built close to an active volcano that erupts periodically. Volcanic mountains, including Mount Fuji in Japan, Mount Rainier in Washington, and Mauna Loa in Hawai‘i, are some of the most recognizable and beautiful mountains in the world. It is no wonder that humans often choose to live near volcanoes, but we should always remember that volcanoes can be dangerous. Volcanoes are home to some of Earth’s most powerful forces. Beautiful Mount Fuji in Japan.
pages.brief: Lava pouring from a volcanic vent creates new rock and land, and volcanic ash makes fertile soil for farming. People use geothermal energy from volcanoes to run power plants and produce electricity. Some live near active volcanoes, such as the port city of Rabaul in Papua New Guinea. Beautiful volcanic mountains include Mount Fuji, Mount Rainier, and Mauna Loa.

pages.brief: A set of small volcanic scenes shows jets of heated water and steam shooting from the ground, a mudslide racing down a volcano, melted rock beneath Earth’s surface, a completely destroyed landscape, a fast superheated cloud, shaking ground, shifting tectonic plates, a volcanologist studying a volcano, and thick syrupy lava.

books.title: Wildlife Rescue
books.art_why: Real wildlife, rehabilitators, and rescue scenes exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: Introduction A baby bird hops along the ground, and its parents are nowhere in sight. What should you do if you observe a baby bird that appears to be orphaned? What if you discover a rabbit that seems unable to hop or a raccoon wobbling and swaying from side to side as it walks? Many people don’t know what actions to take, or not to take, when they find wildlife that may be in need of assistance. However, people with special training in caring for wildlife know exactly what to do. They know to leave the raccoon alone because it is probably sick, and they know whether they can help the rabbit and then return it to the wild. They can also look at the baby bird and determine what care to give, if any. These people can instruct others in how to help, too.
pages.brief: A baby bird hops along the ground with no parent bird visible. Nearby, a rabbit seems unable to hop and a raccoon wobbles and sways as it walks. A person with special wildlife training observes them, ready to decide what care, if any, each animal needs.

pages.text: Wildlife Rehabilitators People who provide aid to sick, injured, or orphaned wildlife are called wildlife rehabilitators, or “rehabbers.” Rehabilitate means “to restore, or bring back, to good health.” Wildlife rehabbers rescue wild animals and care for them as they heal and then release them back into the wild after they recover, whenever possible. These wildlife rehabbers have special training in many areas. Some of them are nutritionists with expertise in what and how much to feed different species of animals. Others are behaviorists, meaning they have studied the behavior of wild animals and can understand and predict what a specific animal will do in various situations. They can also be animal-housing specialists who know exactly the type of cage, pen, or other enclosure to use for different species of animals, especially when an animal is injured and needs a particular kind of shelter to heal safely. Animal caretakers treat a sea turtle for injuries to its right flipper.
pages.brief: Wildlife rehabilitators care for sick, injured, or orphaned wild animals. Some are nutritionists, behaviorists, or animal-housing specialists. In a care setting, animal caretakers treat a sea turtle for injuries to its right flipper, helping it heal before it can be released back into the wild.

pages.text: Common Causes of Injury • Hit by vehicles • Hitting other objects • Poisoning • Illegal hunting • Litter and pollution • Animal attacks Many rehabbers can treat wild animals with illnesses and injuries, too, just as veterinarians do. However, not all rehabbers are veterinarians, and not all veterinarians know how to care for wild animals. Most rehabbers specialize in the capture and transport of injured wildlife, which means that they know how to handle wildlife safely to prevent injury to the animals or themselves. The work of rehabbers is needed more frequently as increasing numbers of people inhabit places where wild animals live. When land is used for farming, houses, and businesses, the natural habitats and foods of wild animals are destroyed, and animals are more likely to be orphaned, injured, or killed. People and their activities cause the majority of wildlife injuries. Rehabber Lisa treats Tripod, a young javelina who was hit by a car. Rehabber Lisa treats Tripod, a young javelina who lost one of its back legs when it was hit by a car.
pages.brief: Rehabber Lisa treats Tripod, a young javelina that lost one of its back legs when a car hit it. The scene shows the injured animal in care, while the page explains common causes of wildlife injury such as vehicles, poisoning, litter, pollution, and animal attacks.

pages.text: Some wildlife rehabbers are generalists; they work with a variety of mammals, birds, and reptiles; but others are specialists, focusing in on just one group of animals, such as owls, bats, or ocean animals. Wildlife rehabbers often care for urban wildlife—animals that live in cities or towns, such as squirrels, raccoons, and foxes. Some courageous rehabbers work with dangerous animals such as bears, mountain lions, and bobcats. Most wildlife rehabbers work with animals that are indigenous, or native to the region where the rehabbers work and live. They have special permits and licenses to treat these animals. To work with exotic animals, which are non-native animals that have migrated or been brought to the region, a rehabber requires special training with those animals as well as special licenses and permits. A Florida state wildlife worker examines a panther kitten.
pages.brief: A Florida state wildlife worker examines a panther kitten. The page explains that some rehabbers are generalists while others specialize in owls, bats, ocean animals, or other groups, and that rehabbers need permits and licenses to treat native and exotic animals.

pages.text: Many wildlife rehabilitation centers specialize in working with particular species, although they communicate with colleagues who specialize in other species in case a different kind of animal is brought in that needs help. You might be wondering how people become wildlife rehabbers. Many rehabbers start as volunteers who learn how to care for animals in the homes and backyards of rehabbers with special wildlife training. Volunteers do not get paid for their work, but most rehabbers do not get paid, either. In fact, rehabbers often spend their own money to buy food, medicine, and shelters for the animals in their care. They are sometimes assisted by donations from people, businesses, and other organizations that also care about wildlife. People help wild animals because they care about animals and want them to get healthy. Rehabbers also recognize that proper care of wild animals promotes healthy habitats and prevents illness and injury to people. A volunteer holds a baby red-tailed hawk while a rehabber takes off a bandage from a leg it broke when it fell out of its nest.
pages.brief: A volunteer holds a baby red-tailed hawk while a rehabber removes a bandage from its leg, broken when the hawk fell out of its nest. The page explains that many rehabbers start as volunteers, often spend their own money on food, medicine, and shelter, and may receive donations.

pages.text: If you encounter an animal that may need rescuing, always follow these two rules: 1) do not touch the animal, and 2) call an adult right away. Adults can help by calling a wildlife rehabber who is trained in wildlife rescue. You can help by watching from a safe place to see where an animal hides so that rescuers can find the animal when they arrive. Putting a cardboard box with small holes or a laundry basket over an injured small animal will protect it from predators until help arrives. Watch Out! If you see any of these animal behaviors, stay away because they are clues that the animal may be sick and dangerous. • a bat on the ground • a wild animal that appears to be tame • an animal with excess drool, or what appears to be foam around its mouth • an animal that can’t move Rescue An animal rescuer gives water to a koala he saved from a wildfire. • an animal that looks extremely angry • a nocturnal animal (one that is normally active at night) that is active during the day— especially a raccoon, skunk, opossum, fox, or bat.
pages.brief: An animal rescuer gives water to a koala saved from a wildfire. The page tells children never to touch a wild animal and to call an adult right away, and it lists warning signs such as a bat on the ground, drooling, or a nocturnal animal active during the day.

pages.text: SAFETY FIRST • Animals may be injured or die from being held incorrectly when they are hurt and frightened. • Animals may be injured or die if kept in the wrong kind of enclosure. For example, wild birds may break bones or damage feathers when trying to escape from wire cages. • Human scent on a baby animal may cause its parents to abandon it. This is truer for mammals than for birds because mammals have a better sense of smell. • Injured wild animals may be frightened because they are in pain. They may bite, kick, scratch, peck, or stab to try to defend themselves, not realizing that people are trying to help. • Wild animals may have diseases that can be passed on to humans and pets. Bats, coyotes, raccoons, foxes, and skunks are more likely than other wild animals to carry rabies, a deadly disease that all warm-blooded animals, including humans, can catch. Anyone who may have been exposed to rabies must be treated right away.
pages.brief: A frightened wild animal bares teeth and raises a paw to bite or scratch while a person stays back at a safe distance. A cage and a baby animal nearby suggest risks from wrong handling, wrong enclosures, and human scent, while a bat, coyote, raccoon, fox, or skunk represents rabies risk.

pages.text: Many baby animals are wrongly, and sometimes tragically, taken from their homes when they aren’t in danger. A baby bird hopping on the ground may not be orphaned—it might be a fledgling, a young bird learning how to fly. Fledglings often hop on the ground to practice moving before they fly and their parents usually watch them, though the parents might not be visible to people. People sometimes think they are rescuing baby rabbits, seals, and deer when these animals aren’t in trouble. It’s normal for babies of these species to rest quietly on a beach or in the grass while their mothers eat nearby. Only people trained in the natural ways of these animals know whether the babies need human assistance; if they don’t, taking them from their mother hurts their chance of survival. Unless baby animals are wounded, they do not need to be rescued.
pages.brief: A fledgling bird hops on the ground while its parents watch from a distance, though people may not see them. Nearby, a baby rabbit, seal, or deer rests quietly in grass or on a beach while its mother eats nearby; the page explains these babies usually do not need rescue.

pages.text: Many people wrongly believe they are helping wild animals by taking them home, but don’t confuse loving wildlife with being able to take care of these animals. Much more training is needed to care for wild animals than to care for dogs and cats—and besides, taking home wild animals is against the law. If you were injured in an accident, would you want just anyone taking you home and caring for you? No, you would want someone trained to help, such as a doctor or nurse. You would also want to be taken to a clean facility that had the appropriate equipment and medicine to help you. Like you, wild animals deserve the best care available. Do You Know? Spring is the busiest time of year for wildlife rescue because wild animals give birth in the spring and babies are weaker and often can’t survive on their own. A baby animal may become orphaned if a car hits its mother or if a hunter or predator kills its parents.
pages.brief: A baby wild animal rests alone in spring, the busiest season for wildlife rescue because babies are weaker and may be orphaned if a car, hunter, or predator kills their mother. The page explains that taking wild animals home is against the law and that trained care is needed.

pages.text: Rehabilitation When animals are brought to a rehabilitation center, the first step is to give them a checkup and first aid. Newly rescued animals are quarantined, or put in their own cages, to prevent them from potentially infecting the other animals. Rehabbers keep detailed notes about each animal so they can tell if the animal is improving, when to give it medicine, and when to feed it. Animals that come to rehabilitation centers can have a wide variety of problems. If they have broken bones or diseases, veterinarians must treat those problems first; afterward the animals can go to the rehabilitation center to rest and get well. Igor, a black vulture, was fed birdseed instead of the meat he needed for good health, so his bones became fragile and broke during his rescue.
pages.brief: At a rehabilitation center, a newly rescued animal receives a checkup and first aid and is quarantined in its own cage. Igor, a black vulture, had fragile bones that broke during rescue because he had been fed birdseed instead of the meat he needed for good health.

pages.text: Animals may need to heal in one place and recover in another place. For example, a hawk with a broken wing might first need a small, dark cage where it can stay calm while it starts to heal. After the broken bone has healed, the hawk might need to move to an outdoor area called a flight cage, where it can exercise and relearn how to fly. Young, injured animals often need additional care so they can heal, and as they become stronger, they may be placed with an adult animal so they can learn from it. Adult animals show younger animals useful behaviors, such as how to hunt for food properly. Rehabilitated birds practice flying in a flight cage until they have healed enough to be released into the wild. Infant animals need special care because they need to stay warm. Rehabbers may put them in an incubator to keep them warm, or the rehabbers may place hot-water bottles, heating pads, or lightbulbs in cages.
pages.brief: A rehabilitated bird practices flying in an outdoor flight cage until it is healed enough for release. Young injured animals may need extra care and can be placed with an adult to learn useful behaviors, while infant animals may stay warm in an incubator or with hot-water bottles, heating pads, or lightbulbs.

pages.text: Most wild animals are frightened of people, and being away from home is stressful. Since too much stress can kill a wild animal, workers at rehabilitation centers try to protect animals from excessive contact with people by keeping noise levels low and covering cages with towels, among other techniques. They also refrain from staring at the animals because, in the wild, staring sends a signal that an animal is being hunted. Imprinting Baby animals imprint on their mothers at an early age; a baby duck learns that it is a duck by watching its mother every day. Wildlife rehabbers take special care not to let baby birds imprint on people; otherwise, the babies will grow up thinking they are human and will seek out humans instead of their own kind. Raptors, or birds of prey, and other birds that have imprinted on people may become dangerous in the wild. For example, they may seek attention from a hiker who doesn’t know they are used to human contact. The hiker or the birds could get hurt in the meeting, so for this reason, the birds often cannot go back to the wild.
pages.brief: A baby duck learns that it is a duck by watching its mother every day. At a rehabilitation center, workers keep noise low and cover cages with towels to reduce stress, and they take special care so baby birds do not imprint on people and later seek out humans instead of their own kind.

pages.text: Do You Know? Meat-eating animals at rehabilitation centers need to eat meat so that they heal and grow strong. Wildlife rehabbers pick up animals recently hit by cars or trucks along roads, called roadkill, to use as animal food. They also keep freezers full of “mouse-cicles”—frozen mice that they use as food. To save money, some centers raise quail, mice, rats, and rabbits as animal food. Wildlife rehabbers must feed each animal its natural foods or something similar because some foods can make the animals sick and hinder their normal growth. For example, cow’s milk is extremely harmful to many baby animals and can even kill them. Rescued animals must be fed natural foods so that they can survive in the wild later on. Natural foods are most important for orphaned animals that have grown up in a rehabilitation center. If they develop a taste for human food or do not learn to hunt or forage on their own, they might starve after being released in the wild.
pages.brief: At a rehabilitation center, meat-eating animals receive meat, including roadkill and frozen mice called mouse-cicles. Some centers raise quail, mice, rats, and rabbits for food. Rescued animals must eat natural foods, because cow's milk can harm babies and human food can leave orphans unable to survive after release.

pages.text: When a rescued animal is ready to return to the wild, rehabbers must decide where to release it. The search for an appropriate location begins long before an animal is ready for release. Knowledge of an animal’s natural history is essential for a rehabber, who must evaluate a potential habitat based on the requirements of the specific animal and the qualities of the location. Rehabbers find an area that has plentiful sources of food, water, and shelter, and they make sure the area is safe from human contact. Rehabbers must also be certain the animal is healthy enough before releasing it—that it can run, climb, swim, or fly without difficulty. They also make sure the animal is able to see, hear, locate food, avoid predators, and be social with other animals of its own kind. When releasing an animal, a rehabber will often request assistance from a wildlife biologist or ornithologist to make sure the process goes smoothly. Release This Tasmanian devil will be examined before it’s released.
pages.brief: A Tasmanian devil will be examined before it is released. Rehabbers choose a release location long in advance, looking for plentiful food, water, shelter, and safety from human contact, and they make sure the animal can run, climb, swim, or fly, find food, avoid predators, and socialize.

pages.text: The first step in releasing an animal is moving it to an outdoor pen or cage with other animals of the same kind. Once outdoors, the animal can get used to the weather and to less-frequent contact with humans until the animal is ready for release. Slow release is often used with young animals, especially orphans. Rehabbers put a pen in a safe place in the wild with the door left open so that the animal can return to it. Rehabbers provide food for the animal until it is clear that the animal can find food for itself. On the other hand, fast release is often used with wild animals rescued as adults because these animals already know how to live on their own in nature. They are taken to a release location, ideally near where they were found, and are let go. A group of onlookers watch as a wildlife rehabber opens the carrier’s door and lets this bald eagle fly free.
pages.brief: A group of onlookers watches as a wildlife rehabber opens a carrier's door and lets a bald eagle fly free. The page explains slow release for young or orphaned animals, which can return to an open pen for food, and fast release for adults that already know how to live in nature.

pages.text: About half the animals at rehabilitation centers are too sick or too badly injured to ever be released back to the wild. Many animals have lost limbs, beaks, wings, or their eyesight. A bird with an injured wing that does not heal properly, or with only one eye, would not be able to fly or hunt in the wild. When it is clear that an animal will never survive in the wild or at a rehabilitation center, rehabbers have to make a difficult decision. If the animal is in pain, euthanasia—quick, painless killing—is sometimes the best way to end that animal’s suffering. This adult female great horned owl is not a quiet flyer because of a wing injury. The noise warns prey animals she hunts, so she can never be released.
pages.brief: An adult female great horned owl has a wing injury that makes her a noisy flyer, warning prey animals she hunts, so she can never be released. The page explains that about half the animals at rehabilitation centers are too sick or badly injured to return to the wild and may need euthanasia if in pain.

pages.text: Disaster Rescue Human activities are not the only causes of wildlife injuries. Natural disasters, such as wildfires, tsunamis, and hurricanes, hurt animals, too. Terri Crisp spends much of her time rescuing animals that are affected by natural disasters. During a raging California wildfire in 1986, Terri rescued a Shetland pony by coaxing it into a car. She worked to save sea otters and loons in 1989 during the Exxon Valdez oil spill in Alaska, and in 1992, she worked to rescue hundreds of animals hurt by Hurricane Andrew. She founded the organization called Noah’s Wish to train volunteers to rescue animals that are at risk because of natural disasters. Terri Crisp holds one of the animals she has rescued from earthquakes, fires, floods, hurricanes, oil spills, tornadoes, and other disasters.
pages.brief: Terri Crisp holds one of the animals she has rescued from earthquakes, fires, floods, hurricanes, oil spills, tornadoes, and other disasters. The page describes her rescue of a Shetland pony during a California wildfire, sea otters and loons after the Exxon Valdez oil spill, and animals hurt by Hurricane Andrew.

pages.text: Incredibly, many wild animals knew to run inland before the 2004 Asian tsunami hit land; however, pets and farm animals did not fare so well. Several people in the areas hit by the tsunami depended on working farm animals; many of these animals were killed, injured, or left in devastated areas without food. The Humane Society International worked with other organizations and volunteers to help the animals—and the people who cared for them— get their lives back on track. A man carries his daughter and their dog to safety through high water after the tsunami in December 2004.
pages.brief: A man carries his daughter and their dog to safety through high water after the December 2004 Asian tsunami. The page explains that many wild animals ran inland before the tsunami, but pets and farm animals suffered, and Humane Society International worked with volunteers to help animals and the people who cared for them.

pages.text: Conclusion Rehabbers often use animals that cannot return to the wild as ambassadors to help teach people to respect wildlife. Children and adults learn about wildlife that live in their local area and about respecting habitats so that wild animals can continue to find food and shelter. Wildlife rehabbers do important work in caring for injured wild animals and returning many of them to the wild. You can help rehabbers’ efforts by respecting wildlife and by calling a rehabber if you see an animal in distress. One phone call might give a wild animal the opportunity to grow up and live a free and healthy life. This bird of prey acts as an ambassador to teach children about animals in their area.
pages.brief: A bird of prey acts as an ambassador, helping teach children about animals in their area. The page explains that rehabbers use animals that cannot return to the wild to teach people to respect wildlife and habitats, and that one phone call to a rehabber can help an animal in distress.
